system_prompt:
You are a mapping assistant backed by a places database (~49M OSM places).

Tools:
- search_places(query?, lat, lng): semantic + lexical search near an anchor you supply from your own knowledge of geography. Use 3-4+ decimal places of precision; one decimal (~11 km) is too coarse and will search the wrong part of a city. Keep query SHORT — a place name or category, no "near X" context. The radius is automatic (tight in cities, wide in wilderness). Misspellings, translations and native scripts all work. Each result shows its neighbourhood or street and town: when a name has several branches, pick the one whose area matches what the user or the page said.
- nearest_places(lat, lng): the closest places around a point, fame-ranked with distance and compass bearing. Use for what's-near and direction questions.
- place_details(refs): address, website, phone, opening hours, fee, wheelchair access, wikipedia link and travel-blog mention count for up to 5 places you already found.
- web_search(query): curated web search over travel writing — real traveler experiences, tips, prices and opinions the places database cannot hold. Use it when the question hinges on what travelers experienced (fees paid, timing, vibe, comparisons).
- web_fetch(url): read the full text of a page returned by web_search.

Rules:
- ALWAYS ground your answer in tool results — never answer a place question from memory alone.
- If the user states their location, use it as the search anchor.
- If searches come up empty or the premise is wrong (place is fictional, demolished, or in a different city than claimed), SAY SO plainly — never present a similarly-named different place as the answer without flagging the difference.
- You have THREE calls of search_places and TWO of web_search and ONE of web_fetch — make each count with your best-formed query. Then fetch a promising page, check details of found refs, or conclude.
- If your attempts fail, say plainly what you could and could not verify. An honest "I couldn't confirm this" is always better than an invented specific.
- Every place you recommend or identify must be RESOLVED in the places database: when a web page names the place, run search_places on that name (a short query, anchored on the city) so you can cite its ref. Search the web first when the question is about vibe, experience or "which place", then resolve the named place. A place answer that cites only a web page is incomplete.
- Finish with a concise plain-text answer naming the specific place(s) you found.
- CREDIT: every web result and fetched page carries a handle like [w2]. Credit a page at the point of use with a markdown link whose target is its handle and whose text is the site or title as shown, e.g. "According to [Full Suitcase](w2), the village is known for ...". Write in your own words; never copy a URL, a coordinate or a run of more than ~25 words from a page. Name places naturally in the prose.
- END with exactly one line: a JSON object {"map": [{"ref": "<ref>"}, ...]} listing the place the answer is about FIRST (its ref from your results), then other places the answer names. When the answer is a JOURNEY, write it as the line it is: place, travel, place — {"map": [{"ref": "<from>"}, {"travel": "walk", "route": "r1"}, {"ref": "<to>"}]}, where the travel node names the mode and the handle of the calculate_route result your numbers came from ([r1], [r2] ... in the tool output). A travel node always sits BETWEEN two places — never first, never last. When the journey starts where the user is, that first node is {"here": true}, e.g. {"map": [{"here": true}, {"travel": "walk", "route": "r1"}, {"ref": "<to>"}]}. Put places you merely mention in "mentions": [{"ref": ...}] instead of the line. {"map": []} if no place is cited. That object is the last line of your answer, on its own, with no code fence and nothing after it. Never write bare handles like [w1] in the prose; the handle only ever appears as a link target. Example ending:
  ...open daily until 5 pm according to [Travel Lemming](w3).
  {"map": [{"ref": "<ref of that place from your search results>"}]}

  ÚĽUV is also one of the organisations behind the Christmas Forest project. There is nothing slow about our next activity that day. In a 600-year-old cellar right next to Michael’s Gate, Kustar’s Music Band entertains us with some traditional Slovak folk music at the Folklore Garden Restaurant.
[w2] Traveling to Bratislava: Getting in touch with my inner Marxist — johnhendersontravel.com
  Recovering from a Slivovice hangover in Poprad, the author visits Bratislava’s Old Town, eating at Bumbalka tavern and walking through Michael’s Gate.
  The moment I laid down, my room started to spin like I was stuck inside a blender making margaritas in a biker bar near Juarez. I didn’t know what European historical period I was in. If Stalin had marched Soviet troops into my room I would’ve gladly surrendered if he had a cure for the violent earthquake Slivovice put in my stomach and head. (A very under-appreciated amenity in my pension: The toilet can flush numerous times in two minutes. Think about it.) So pulling a repeat in Bratislava wasn’t on my agenda last night. My hangover had mercilessly disappeared about halfway to town and an intense hunger replaced it. On the way into Bratislava’s Old Town, a found a sprawling outdoor tavern called Bumbalka. It was filled with outdoor picnic tables and Budvar (Budweiser’s paternal father) signs. If they played country-western music instead of American oldies it would’ve passed for a great Texas BBQ joint. Instead, it was just an authentic little local watering hole with typically Slovak food. Slovakia is dirt cheap. I haven’t paid more than 2.20 euros for a beer, never more than 5 euros for a meal. For 3.50 at Bumbalka, I had a bean soup, breaded chicken and a big pile of boiled potatoes. A Budvar (so good you wonder how American breweries screwed up Budweiser) was only 90 cents. A stroll through Old Town made me glad I made this detour. I passed under a huge arch of Michael’s Gate, featuring a 14th century base and a pointy 18th century tower that looks like a witch’s loft. Inside the gate, Old Town is a pedestrian-only collage of outdoor bars, restaurants and souvenir shops. It’s over-the-top touristy.

  Exploring the Roland Fountain and Michael’s Gate in Bratislava’s Old Town, including the latter’s history as a medieval city entrance and coronation route.
  Another interesting landmark in the Main Square is the Roland Fountain (Rolandova fontána in Slovak). It was built by Maximilan II in the 16th century, making it the most popular fountain in Bratislava. ## Stroll Through Michael’s Gate If you’re looking to explore the Old Town of Bratislava, you’re undoubtedly going to walk through Michael’s Gate (Michalská brána in Slovak) at some point. This 14th century gate is a very famous landmark in Bratislava due to its historical value – it’s the only medieval city gate in the Old Town that still stands. Back in the old days, there used to be walls surrounding the town and protecting it, and Michael’s Gate was one of the four gates that allowed people to enter and leave the town. What’s more, the gate used to play an important role in the coronation process. It used to be one of the places kings had to pass through on their way to take an oath. Nowadays, the gate is a popular tourist attraction. There’s a museum inside where you can learn more about the medieval fortification of Bratislava, as well as what weapons have been used here throughout history. However, the Museum of Weapons has been officially closed from December 2020 due to renovation. The closure is supposed to last for about two years.
[w5] 24 hours in Bratislava | The perfect itinerary | Hidden gems and must dos
  Dining at Flag Ship restaurant in Bratislava to sample traditional Slovak dishes like bryndzové halušky and kapustnica.
  Hours of operation: 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., Mondays closed. Cost: €5 ## 7 p.m. Eat Slovakian delicacies at a local restaurant Slovakian delicacies are many, but if you have to prioritise, try the halušky and the Kapustnica. Halušky, the Slovak national dish, are boiled dumplings made from grated raw potato dough. When served with bryndza, a sheep’s milk cheese, the dish is called *bryndzové halušky*. Another staple of Slovak cuisine is *kapustnica*, a traditional cabbage soup. Try the dishes at the inexpensive Flag Ship restaurant at Námestie SNP 8. While service can be tardy, the food is quite good. Add a glass of Tatra Tea to top it up.

The temple you're looking for is **Kunj Bihari Mandir** (listed in the places database as Kunj Bihari Ji Temple), in the Katla Bazar temple square just off the Clock Tower Market in Jodhpur's old city.

According to [Rama Toshi Arya's blog](w1), this 18th-century temple is dedicated to Krishna and was commissioned by Gulab Rai, the favourite concubine of Maharaja Vijay Singh. The blog notes that a mural high on the wall of the mandapa (main hall) depicts her and the Maharaja together as a legitimate couple, expressing devotion to the Krishna Vallabha cult — a striking public statement of the political clout and love she commanded. The temple is guarded by an imposing marble toran and topped with a towering shikhara, and at first glance resembles the nearby Shri Gangshyam Ji Mandir. The same author also mentions it in her [36 Hours in Jodhpur](w2) piece as "Jodhpur's famed concubine Gulab Rai's public statement of political clout and love."

The database entry gives its address as Katla Chowk, Katla Bazar, Jodhpur, with a contact number of +91 95093 05607.

[w1] stepwells and temples of jodhpur’s old city | rama toshi arya's blog
  Exploring the Kunj Bihari Mandir, commissioned by concubine Gulab Rai, and Achal Nath Shivalaya, Jodhpur’s oldest Shiva temple, in the city’s temple square.
  # Kunj Bihari Mandir, Gulab Rai’s statement of power and love Close to Jodhpur’s Clock Tower Market is the crowded temple square lined on all four sides by temples interspersed with stalls selling colourful garlands, fragrant incense sticks, and busy sweetmeat shops. One particular temple deserves special mention here: the 18th Century **Kunj Bihari Mandir** dedicated to Krishna. Gulab Rai, Maharaja Vijay Singh’s favourite concubine, commissioned the temple. Guarded by an imposing marble *toran* and topped with a towering *shikhara*, it appears at first glance to be a copy of Shri Gangshyam Ji Mandir. If ever there was a doubt about the powers a concubine could weld, the Kunj Bihari Mandir puts it to rest. A mural high up on the wall in the mandapa or main hall depicts her and the Maharaja, as a legitimate couple, expressing their devotion to the Krishna Vallabha cult. # Achal Nath Shivalaya, Jodhpur city’s oldest Shiva temple One last temple that requires inclusion in this post is the double shivling **Achal Nath Shivalaya** in the temple square. In a society which comprises predominantly of Krishna followers, temples to Shiva are far and few in Jodhpur. Which is where Achal Nath Shivalaya comes in. Built by Nanak Devi, Rao Ganga Rathore’s queen in 1531, it is also Jodhpur’s oldest Shiva temple. Despite being plastered over in recent years with ceramic tiles—an aesthetic sacrilege that has not made any dent to its sanctity—devotees flock to it with much fervour, their murmured chants accompanied with ringing bells and incense smoke. Like all Hindu temples, Achal Nath Shivalaya includes shrines to other Hindu deities as well. Of particular significance is the **Shrine of Baba Ramdev** to its right, Rajasthan’s most popular indigenous deity.
[w2] 36 hours in jodhpur, capital of the kingdom of marwar | rama toshi arya's blog
  Exploring Jodhpur’s non-touristy side around Ghanta Ghar through historical stepwells like Toorji Ka Jhalra and evocative temples such as Achal Nath Shivalaya.
  Why? Because it offers a unique opportunity to get under the city’s touristy mantle and instead feel it’s pulse amidst local legends and stories galore. Unlike Navchokiya, which is the neighbourhood expressly for the Brahmins or priests in Jodhpur, the area on the other side of the fort is inhabited by the Rajputs, Ravana Rajputs, and other castes. It is this area which is the focus of the second walk. Dotted with **historical stepwells** around **Ghanta Ghar or the Clock Tower**, each water reservoir has a story to tell. There’s **Gulab Sagar**, a wealthy concubine’s gift to Jodhpur, **Mahila Bagh Jhalra**, an Irishman’s ‘clean-up’ mission, **Tapi Baori**, Jodhpur’s secret stepwell, and **Toorji Ka Jhalra**, the city’s public swimming pool. Jodhpur’s temples in this part of town are no less evocative, with a tantalizing mix of tales and art. They include **Shri Gangshyam Ji Mandir**, a temple built specially to house a Queen’s personal idol of Krishna. There’s **Kunj Bihari Mandir**, Jodhpur’s famed concubine Gulab Rai’s public statement of political clout and love. And lastly, **Achal Nath Shivalaya**, Jodhpur’s oldest Shiva temple which warrants a visit for its double shivling and the shrine of Baba Ramdev inside. **Baba Ramdev aka Ramdeo Pir** is Rajasthan’s most popular local deity spanning religion and borders, royalty and plebs, humanity and divinity, and is found all over the desert State.
[w3] A Backpacker's Guide to Jodhpur - Man Vs Globe
  Dining on Rajasthani thalis at the rooftop of Nirvana Hotel, located opposite the Clock Tower in Jodhpur.
  **Where**: 1 Pal Haveli Inn Opposite the Clock Tower**When**: 9.30am – 10.30pm Daily ### Nirvana When we were sat on the rooftop of Nirvana Hotel in the dark, the only diners in this vast space overlooking Tambaku Bazar, I wasn’t expecting much from my meal. However, the Thali that I was served ended up being one of the best I had in Jodhpur. Nirvana shares a building with a Rama temple and a kitsch hotel of the same name. Although there is both an outdoor and indoor dining area, I recommend heading up to the roof for your meal.
[w4] My 2 days in Jodhpur | Best places to visit in Jodhpur in 2 days - Thrilling Travel
  Scenic views of langur monkeys near Mandore Gardens and exploring the London-made Clock Tower in Jodhpur.
  On the road that leads to Mandore Gardens, there is lush greenery. There are small ponds also, and many langur monkeys frolicking around. You can take so many selfies here and pose in the background of one of these temples. It will make your Instagram profile extremely photogenic. ### Clock Tower area – Ghanta Ghar The Clock Tower of Jodhpur is also called Ghanta Ghar, which is quite famous in Jodhpur. The Clock Tower is the first monument that I also visited on my 2 days Jodhpur sightseeing tour and even today this clock shows the correct time. It is said that the Clock Tower was made in London and installed here on the orders of a maharaja. The architecture of the Clock Tower is what is most interesting. It looks like some French or Paris monument. I was thrilled to go up this Clock Tower and see the entire area from the top. The topmost floor has the actual clock with all its machinery. You can see the entire clock and the man who operates it also sits by the clock.

The attraction you're describing is **Reptile Gardens**, just south of Rapid City on US Highway 16 toward Mount Rushmore.

It matches your description point for point. According to [Daytripper28](w2), it's "a family-friendly stop packed with unique exhibits featuring snakes, alligators, and other exotic creatures," and it also has tropical gardens, interactive shows, and a giant tortoise encounter. [Cinder's Travels](w3) notes it was founded by a 1930s reptile enthusiast who wanted to help tourists get over their fear of snakes, and that it's now billed as the largest reptile zoo in the world — with dozens of interactive exhibits plus non-reptiles like a laughing kookaburra, a bald eagle, and a prairie dog town. A family travel blog, [Vagabond3](w1), describes kids getting to touch a 50-year-old tortoise there, and [One Girl, Whole World](w4) flags it as a solid pick if you're traveling with children.

Practical details from the database: it's at 8955 South Highway 16, Rapid City, SD 57702, phone +1 605-342-5873, website reptilegardens.com, and there is an admission fee. It sits about 10.5 km south of downtown Rapid City, roughly 25 minutes by car. Note that it's a seasonal park — open from early March through November 30 — so it's a warm-weather stop.

**Cara Feliz** is the place you're looking for — it's the one cafe in Tulum pueblo that combines all three things you asked for.

According to [Your Friend the Nomad](w1), Cara Feliz is a "sleepy bookstore with coffee and brunch" set just off Tulum pueblo's main street, described as quiet and light-filled, with a small but ample selection of books in both English and Spanish. Crucially, the same source notes that most Tulum cafes are outdoor-only, but Cara Feliz has indoor seating with air conditioning — exactly the hot-day hideout you want. It's open 8am–10pm daily, and the menu runs to a breakfast sandwich with chipotle aioli and vegan brownies.

I resolved it in the places database: Cara Feliz sits on Beta Norte in the Manuel Antonio Ay area of Tulum Centro, about 360 m from the pueblo's centre, phone +52 984 801 1531.

A couple of nearby alternatives if you want a backup, though neither is book-focused:
- **Botanica Garden Cafe** (Andrómeda Oriente, ~965 m away) — a garden cafe with the most travel-blog mentions of any cafe in the pueblo.
- **Alfonsina Coffee**, which [Tulum Travel](w5) singles out for its chic, cosy, air-conditioned indoor area on Guerra de Castas in Tulum Centro — good for AC, but no book selection mentioned.

Worth flagging: there's no dedicated bookstore in Tulum pueblo itself — the nearest proper bookshops are in Valladolid, Puerto Morelos and Mérida. The town's public library, Biblioteca Pública Municipal "Jacinto Pat", is about 440 m from the centre if you just want somewhere to read.

rows.final:
**Short answer: the Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade — the whole waterfront strip from the Star Ferry Pier and Clock Tower east to the Avenue of Stars.**

Why it works: this stretch of the Kowloon shore faces south/southwest straight across Victoria Harbour at the Hong Kong Island skyline, so you get the skyscrapers of Central and Admiralty head-on, with the sun dropping behind the island and the lights coming on as it goes. According to [Becky Exploring](w1), arriving in late afternoon lets you watch the sun set behind the island and see the city lights gradually switch on — she suggests walking from the Clock Tower toward the harbour. [Muy Linda Travels](w5) likewise calls the promenade a beautiful place to watch the sunset over the harbour, and notes it's where the Avenue of Stars sits, with the free "Symphony of Lights" laser show at 8 pm nightly.

Specific spots along it, west to east:

- **Tsim Sha Tsui Star Ferry Pier / Clock Tower area** — the classic postcard angle, right by the ferry concourse and the old clock tower. The promenade garden here is the most blogged section of the walk (26 travel-blog mentions in the database).
- **Kowloon Public Pier** — a small viewpoint jutting out just south of the Clock Tower, good for an unobstructed, uncrowded frame of the island.
- **Hong Kong Cultural Centre** forecourt — the wide open plaza behind the Clock Tower, a favourite for photographers because nothing blocks the view.
- **Avenue of Stars (East Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront)** — the eastern end, with the Bruce Lee statue and film-star handprints. [Just An Ordinary Girl](w3) describes this East Waterfront stretch as offering a stunning, unobstructed panorama of Central across the harbour, and it's especially good after dark.

Practical notes: the promenade is free and open 24 hours, and [Solo Backpacker](w4) reckons you should allow a couple of hours to walk it properly from the Star Ferry Pier to the InterContinental end. To get there, take the MTR to Tsim Sha Tsui (exit L6) and walk toward the Clock Tower, or ride the Star Ferry across from Central — the crossing itself is a cheap harbour cruise.

One caveat: because the promenade faces the island, the sun sets *behind* the skyline rather than over open water, so the best light is the 30–45 minutes before and after sunset, when the buildings silhouette and then light up.

**Short answer: the Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade — the whole waterfront strip from the Star Ferry Pier and Clock Tower east to the Avenue of Stars.**

Why it works: this stretch of the Kowloon shore faces south/southwest straight across Victoria Harbour at the Hong Kong Island skyline, so you get the skyscrapers of Central and Admiralty head-on, with the sun dropping behind the island and the lights coming on as it goes. - **Avenue of Stars (East Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront)** — the eastern end, with the Bruce Lee statue and film-star handprints. [Just An Ordinary Girl](w3) describes this East Waterfront stretch as offering a stunning, unobstructed panorama of Central across the harbour, and it's especially good after dark.

## The Maine State House, Augusta

**Yes — it's worth a brief stop, and your impression is accurate.** The building at 210 State Street is indeed one of the plainer state capitols, which makes sense once you know its history.

**The "understated" part is real.** It was designed by Charles Bulfinch of Boston and completed in 1832, deliberately modeled on his Massachusetts State House — Maine had just split from Massachusetts in 1820, and the first capital was Portland before Augusta's more central location won out. It's built of granite quarried in nearby Hallowell, roughly 150 feet long originally. Travelers who've made the stop describe it in the same terms you did: [No Home Just Roam](w1) called it "more understated than many we've seen, with a less ornate dome than some," and [Wandering Jana](w2) found it "much plainer than I thought it would be like and much smaller," noting it was a nice visit that didn't take long.

**About the dome** — the honest answer is that it's a replacement, added later. The original Bulfinch design had only a cupola; the dome you'll see was built in the 1909–1910 remodel by G. Henri Desmond, which doubled the building's length to 300 feet and demolished nearly everything except the front and rear walls. The dome rises to 185 feet and is topped by a gilt copper statue of Minerva, the figure of wisdom, by William Clark Noble of Gardiner. So it's a 20th-century dome grafted onto a Federal-style Bulfinch front — part of why it reads as less ornate than, say, a gilded gold dome elsewhere.

One quirk worth knowing: the dome's copper sheathing was replaced in 2014 because it was pockmarked with hail damage and corrosion. It will look browner than green for roughly 35 years until the copper re-oxidizes to its familiar verdigris — so depending on your visit, the color may not be what postcards show.

**Practical notes:** the State House is open weekdays 08:00–17:00, phone +1-207-287-1692, website legislature.maine.gov. It's on the National Register of Historic Places and is the only known Bulfinch work with a complete surviving set of architectural drawings — a small architectural-buff bonus.

**Worth pairing with your stop:** the Maine State Museum is a 2-minute walk away at 230 State Street, and the Maine State Library sits right there too. Across the street to the north is the Executive Mansion, the Blaine House. Given it's a leg of a Bangor-to-Portland drive, a 30–45 minute stretch of the legs, a photo of the Bulfinch front, and a peek at the Hall of Flags is a fair return — just don't expect the grandeur of a Vermont or Massachusetts capitol.

[w6] Maine State House (Wikipedia)
The Maine State House in Augusta, Maine, is the state capitol of the State of Maine. The building was completed in 1832, one year after Augusta became the capital of Maine. Built using Maine granite, the State House was based on the design of the Massachusetts State House (Maine was formerly part of Massachusetts, and became a separate state in 1820). Governor Janet Mills and the Maine Legislature convene at the State House. When Maine separated from Massachusetts and became a state in 1820, a number of cities and towns sought the honor of becoming the state capital. The principal aspirants were Portland, Brunswick, Hallowell, Waterville, Belfast, Wiscasset, and Augusta. The first capital of Maine was Portland, but it moved to Augusta because of its more central location. The Legislature passed and Governor Samuel E. Smith signed the bill establishing Augusta as the capital in 1832. After careful consideration of various sites on both sides of the river, the governor and the Commissions chose a 34 acres (140,000 m2) lot for the Maine State House and extending from the old Hallowell road to the Kennebec River. The building was designed by the renowned architect Charles Bulfinch of Boston, and in its original form resembles his Massachusetts State House. About 150 feet (46 m) in length, including the central portion with columns and cupola and two wings extending north and south, the building's cornerstone was laid on July 4, 1829, amid impressive Masonic ceremonies. Construction was of granite from Hallowell quarries and took three years to complete. The cost of the building was originally estimated to be $80,000, but when completed, expenditures of the building, furnishings and grounds amounted to $135,000, of which $11,500 was contributed by the city of Augusta. The Maine Legislature held its first session in the new state Capitol on January 4, 1832. The interior of the Capitol was remodeled in 1852 and again in 1860 to provide additional room for state departments. In 1890–1891, a large three-story wing was added to the rear of the building to accommodate the State Library and to provide more office space for departments. Major remodeling of the Capitol during 1909–1910 established the present-day appearance of the building. It was enlarged according to designs by G. Henri Desmond, necessitating the demolition of almost all the old buildings save the front and rear walls. While the noble Bulfinch front was preserved, the length of the building was doubled to 300 feet (91 m) by extending the north and south wings. A dome rising to a height of 185 feet (56 m) was built to replace the original cupola. A gilt copper statue of Minerva, the draped female figure of Wisdom, by William Clark Noble of Gardiner, surmounted the dome. The House of Representatives occupies the third and fourth floors of the north wing and the Senate chambers occupy similar quarters in the south wing. The governor's office is located in renovated space on the second floor at the rear of the central portion of the Capitol along with the Hall of Flags and the law library. The governor's office overlooks the massive, granite State Office Building located to the west of the State House. A recently renovated tunnel connects the State House and the State Office Building. The tunnel houses several Maine wildlife scenes. A side tunnel leads to a cold war fallout shelter, large enough to house the Maine senate, house and various other officials and aides. Construction of the shelter started on May 5, 1983, under the pretense of renovation; completed September 3, 1985, and it has been fully stocked and staffed ever since.[citation needed] At the south side of the Capitol grounds, the Maine State Library, Maine State Museum and Maine State Archives are housed in a modern building. Throughout the building are portraits of governors and other men and women who have served Maine throughout its history as a province and a state. To the north, across from the State House, is the Executive Mansion, more commonly known as The Blaine House, which Harriet Blaine Beale presented to the state in 1919. The State House was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973, for its importance in the history of the state, and for its architecture. It is the only known work of Charles Bulfinch for which a complete set of architectural drawings has survived. On August 15, 2022, a large metal object traveling at a high speed crashed onto the Capitol grounds, narrowly missing a Maine Capitol Police employee. The incident prompted an investigation by the Federal Aviation Administration. The Maine Legislature's Legislative Council authorized the replacement of the copper sheath of the dome, which was long past its intended 75-year lifespan when it was installed in 1909–1910. The copper was pockmarked with hail damage and corrosion, with some holes in it as large as a dime. The eight-month project commenced in March 2014 and completed in October. The dome appears exactly the same as prior to renovations, with the exception of the color; it will appear brown for approximately 35 years until the copper oxidizes to a green once again. The statue of Minerva was also re-gilded and repaired by EverGreene Architectural Arts. The cost of $1.2 million was paid from a Legislative Council account. The replacement of the copper was completed October 1, with some minor work lasting until November. Legislative leaders placed a time capsule in the dome, containing a book of Maine laws, a legislative handbook, the September 30 issue of the Kennebec Journal, some of the old copper, and personal items from the legislators. The Legislative Council debated what to do with the old copper roof once it was removed from the dome. The contract for the project originally called for the State to have salvage rights for 500 square feet (46 m2) of the old copper and the contractor to have rights to the remainder, which has an estimated value of $15,000. It had been suggested that the State may want to keep more of the copper in order to do more with it. Democratic Assistant Senate Majority Leader Anne Haskell has suggested that at least some of the copper could be sold or auctioned to Mainers who might want a memento of the building, such as former state workers or legislators. She also suggested some sort of contest could be held among artists for using the copper, perhaps as part of the State's "one percent for art" program. Republican Senate Minority Leader Michael Thibodeau stated his support for some sort of artistic use of the copper but expressed concern about how the copper would be stored, storage costs, and security. On September 24, the Council decided to purchase the 6,500 square feet (600 m2) of old copper from the contractor and will make some into souvenirs and sell about 600 square feet (56 m2) to artists for the making of art and the remainder will be scrapped. It is conservatively expected that the portion sold to artists will bring approximately $12,250 to the State, while the making of souvenirs will cost about $3,600. Legislative leaders believe the State could make more money than estimated. ## The Maine State House, Augusta

**Yes — it's worth a brief stop, and your impression is accurate.** The building at 210 State Street is indeed one of the plainer state capitols, which makes sense once you know its history.

**The "understated" part is real.** It was designed by Charles Bulfinch of Boston and completed in 1832, deliberately modeled on his Massachusetts State House — Maine had just split from Massachusetts in 1820, and the first capital was Portland before Augusta's more central location won out. It's built of granite quarried in nearby Hallowell, roughly 150 feet long originally. Travelers who've made the stop describe it in the same terms you did: [No Home Just Roam](w1) called it "more understated than many we've seen, with a less ornate dome than some," and [Wandering Jana](w2) found it "much plainer than I thought it would be like and much smaller," noting it was a nice visit that didn't take long.

**About the dome** — the honest answer is that it's a replacement, added later. The original Bulfinch design had only a cupola; the dome you'll see was built in the 1909–1910 remodel by G. Henri Desmond, which doubled the building's length to 300 feet and demolished nearly everything except the front and rear walls. The dome rises to 185 feet and is topped by a gilt copper statue of Minerva, the figure of wisdom, by William Clark Noble of Gardiner. So it's a 20th-century dome grafted onto a Federal-style Bulfinch front — part of why it reads as less ornate than, say, a gilded gold dome elsewhere.

One quirk worth knowing: the dome's copper sheathing was replaced in 2014 because it was pockmarked with hail damage and corrosion. It will look browner than green for roughly 35 years until the copper re-oxidizes to its familiar verdigris — so depending on your visit, the color may not be what postcards show.

**Practical notes:** the State House is open weekdays 08:00–17:00, phone +1-207-287-1692, website legislature.maine.gov. It's on the National Register of Historic Places and is the only known Bulfinch work with a complete surviving set of architectural drawings — a small architectural-buff bonus.

**Worth pairing with your stop:** the Maine State Museum is a 2-minute walk away at 230 State Street, and the Maine State Library sits right there too. Across the street to the north is the Executive Mansion, the Blaine House. Given it's a leg of a Bangor-to-Portland drive, a 30–45 minute stretch of the legs, a photo of the Bulfinch front, and a peek at the Hall of Flags is a fair return — just don't expect the grandeur of a Vermont or Massachusetts capitol.

The alpine coaster at Breckenridge is the **Gold Runner Alpine Coaster** (often written "GoldRunner"), which runs down from the Peak 8 base area at Breckenridge Ski Resort — the database lists it on Four O'Clock Run Road in Breckenridge, about 2.5 km from the town centre.

It's a single- or two-person cart on an elevated track where you control your own speed, and it's known for its hairpin curves through the trees. According to [365 Atlanta Traveler](w3), the GoldRunner "offers a thrilling ride through forest hairpin curves," and the same site's Breckenridge guide describes the mountain's coaster-style ride as a 2,500-foot descent around and through the Rocky Mountains to the base of the peak ([365 Atlanta Traveler](w1)).

Don't confuse it with the Alpine Super Slide, a separate summer luge/toboggan attraction also in Breckenridge, or with Vail's Forest Flyer Alpine Coaster ([The World Pursuit](w2)).

The alpine coaster at Breckenridge is the **Gold Runner Alpine Coaster** (often written "GoldRunner"), which runs down from the Peak 8 base area at Breckenridge Ski Resort — the database lists it on Four O'Clock Run Road in Breckenridge, about 2.5 km from the town centre.

It's a single- or two-person cart on an elevated track where you control your own speed, and it's known for its hairpin curves through the trees. According to [365 Atlanta Traveler](w3), the GoldRunner "offers a thrilling ride through forest hairpin curves," and the same site's Breckenridge guide describes the mountain's coaster-style ride as a 2,500-foot descent around and through the Rocky Mountains to the base of the peak ([365 Atlanta Traveler](w1)).

Don't confuse it with the Alpine Super Slide, a separate summer luge/toboggan attraction also in Breckenridge, or with Vail's Forest Flyer Alpine Coaster ([The World Pursuit](w2)).

For stepping back into law-making history in Sacramento, the place to go is the **California State Capitol Museum**, housed inside the historic State Capitol building at 1315 10th Street in Downtown Sacramento.

It's the right pick because the museum occupies the restored 19th-century Capitol itself — you walk the same halls where California's legislature has met, and the exhibits cover the state's political and legislative history, with restored historic offices and rooms. It sits right beside the working **California State Capitol** (the active government seat), so you get both the living institution and the museum interpretation in one visit.

If you want to broaden the theme, **The California Museum** (1020 O Street, a few blocks away) covers broader California history and civics, including the state's constitution and governance — open Tuesday–Saturday 10–5 and Sunday 12–5, with an admission fee.

The brewery you're thinking of is **Lakefront Brewery**, at **1872 North Commerce Street, Milwaukee** — in the Beerline B neighborhood along the Milwaukee River, just north of downtown. Its beer hall sits right beside it on North Holton Street.

The background matches exactly: according to [Beyond The Miles Travel Blog](w2), the brewery has been operating since 1987, was started by two brothers using mostly second-hand equipment, and got a piece of machinery seen in the opening credits of *Laverne & Shirley* from the old Schlitz Brewery (the show's fictional Shotz Brewery was a stand-in for Schlitz). The founders were brothers Russ and Jim Klisch — Russ, an engineer, and Jim, a Milwaukee police officer, who began with a 55-gallon drum setup in an old bakery, as Russ recounted on [The Royal Tour](w4). The Laverne & Shirley connection still lives on in the tour: [No Home Just Roam](w1) describes visitors singing the show's theme while someone places a glove on a bottle in the bottling room — and it's widely rated the best brewery tour in the city ([The Planet D](w3)).

It's open Monday–Thursday 11 am–8 pm, Friday 11 am–9 pm, Saturday 9 am–9 pm and Sunday 10 am–5 pm.

**Short answer: the Tharu Cultural Museum in Bachhauli, on the northern edge of Sauraha (Ratnanagar-07).**

It's the place to go for both things you asked about. The museum sits in the Tharu village of Bachhauli, about 800 m north-east of Sauraha's tourist strip — the nearest landmark cluster to the museum is the hamlet of Bachhauli itself, and the Sauraha suburb centre is roughly 570 m south-west of it. Inside, the collection displays the tools and traditional clothing the Tharu use in the fields, and the site includes a model/replica of a traditional Tharu home — the long mud-and-reed houses the community is known for. There's an entry fee.

A few practical notes from travelers:

- The village around the museum is a real, lived-in Tharu settlement of mud-and-reed huts, not a staged set. According to [The Longest Way Home](w4), it's about a 30–40 minute walk (roughly 2 km) from central Sauraha, flat and easy by bicycle (rentals around NPR 200 for a half day), and there's no charge to walk through the village itself — only the museum charges. The same guide notes the village's small museum displays field tools and traditional clothes, and that quiet independent visitors may even be invited in for tea.
- Guided half-day tours from Sauraha agents run about NPR 400 per person, or NPR 800–1,200 by pony or ox cart, but the village stop on those tours is brief.
- For seeing Tharu dress *worn* rather than displayed, the evening cultural dance programme in Sauraha is the complement: performers appear in black blouses and white saris, or white-and-red shirts with dhoti, as described by [Azure Sky Follows](w2). [The Longest Way Home](w1) notes the show runs nightly from about 7 pm and includes the peacock dance, and [Third Eye Traveller](w5) confirms the Tharu cultural house show is the standard evening activity in town.

So: museum in Bachhauli for the dress exhibits and replica house by day, the evening dance show in Sauraha for dress in performance.

## About the Tharu

The Tharu are an **ethnic group indigenous to the Terai region of Nepal** which includes Chitwan. Nearly 7% of Nepal's population are Tharu. The Tharu in Chitwan have lived there for hundreds of years and call themselves **"The People of the Forest"**. They farm rice, corn, lentil, and hunt wild boar, deer, rabbit along with river fish. Unlike a lot of Nepal's population, the Tharu are not known to seek employment overseas. Thusly, the Tharu have brought up a unique culture and way of life unlike other tribes in Nepal. Hidden Insights

#### 
          Uncovered Corner:

 Tharu Village in Chitwan
        

      
        ** Why is this an Uncovered Corner?**

Just a 30-minute walk or bicycle ride from touristy Sauraha lies a genuine Tharu village of long mud-and-reed homes where the “People of the Forest” still live as they have for centuries. Most visitors are whisked through on quick 
		tours, missing the chance to wander freely, greet families. If you arrive quietly without a tour, you'll be more likely to see what the village really is like.
      

#### Responsible Travel

        **Travel with Purpose: Go Deeper.

** I advocate visiting the Tharu village independently (walk or bicycle) rather than on rushed group tours. Arriving respectfully and quietly puts money directly into local hands through bicycle rentals, small purchases, or spontaneous homestay invitations—supporting a proud community that has chosen to stay rooted in their land instead of seeking work abroad.

| Did you know? The  There is no one Tharu language. Instead there variants depending on the location of the village. Most speak a variant of Hindi/Urdu and Awadhi.

| As you will read later you don't have to restrict yourself to visiting Tharu in Chitwan alone. What makes Chitwan special is that **the village located right next to Sauraha** town itself where most tourists stay.

## How to visit the Tharu village in Chitwan

There are **three main ways to see the Tharu village** (Badrahani) near Sauraha in Chitwan.

- Take a regular tour
- Take an ox cart tour
- Walk or bicycle there independently

Take a regular tour: Nearly **all travel agents in Sauraha**, including hotels, **offer half-day tours** around Sauraha via a mini-van or jeep. This will include a visit to the Tharu village, the elephant breeding center and some local artisans. Costs depend on the itinerary but are generally around 400 rupees per person. Keep in mind the actual village visit is quite short. Take an ox or pony cart tour: this method has become increasingly popular in recent years. It's basically the same as the above tour but instead of motorized transport **you'll be on an ox drawn cart or pony cart**. It's a fun and eco-friendly way to get around Sauraha and visit the Tharu village.

Prices start at about the same rate of 1,200 for an ox cart or 800 rupees for a pony cart. **Larger groups are preferred** but you can hire one privately.

Walk or Bicycle: The **Tharu village is only about a 30-40 minute walk (2km) from the center of Sauraha**. It's a flat walk so taking a bicycle will be easy and quicker. The cost of renting a bicycle is negotiable but an average price for a half-day is about 200 rupees. There's no entrance fee into the actual village itself. However, the villagers are more used to tour groups visiting. So if you arrive when a tour is not there you may not get to talk to anyone who speaks English or have someone show you around.

## What can you see at the Tharu Village? The village itself is **comprised of several mud and reed huts**. Domestic and farm animals roam around or are in enclosures. It's a basic place where people really do live and work. There's a **small museum** there which displays the tools and traditional clothes people use out in the field. The amount of interaction you will have with the Tharu people living there is dependent on how many tourists are visiting when you are. **Most Tharu are busy with their daily lives** but will be happy to say hello (Namaste) to you should you greet them. On quiet days independent travelers might be lucky enough to be invited inside a person's home for a cup of tea.

## Directions to the Tharu village

By foot or bicycle: From the main Sauraha road simply **walk to the elephant statue and take a left**. Continue along this **main road until you get to an open field area** with a dirt road going straight while the main road turns right (towards the elephant jungle tour area). **Take the dirt road** and keep going straight. The **Tharu village will be on your left** after about 20 mins. Keep going!: For a longer day out after visiting the village stay on the dirt road and continue on to the Elephant Breeding Centre. ## Is the Tharu village worth visiting? It really **depends on you**, **your time frame**, and **what you've seen before**. If you've **never seen a local Nepali or Tharu village before then yes it's a nice trip**. **If you have seen local villages before then there's not too much to get excited about** at all. It's certainly not worth it as a single destination tour. Mixed in with other things then yes, it's a worthy addition. If you are going independently by yourself then it's certainly worth popping into on the way to the Elephant breeding center or if you have some time to spare. There are other similar villages to the east and south of Sauraha if you take an extended walk. By walking yourself you will also come across private elephant stables, local farms, small communities and get a closer look at the real Chitwan. Again, if you have time this would be, in my opinion, a better option that a tour. If you do opt for a tour, then be prepared to pay extra for it as you'll largely be paying for transport via a tour company.

Travelers visiting the rest of Nepal may not find much interest in a Tharu village as it's pretty similar to a local farm village. However, if you are on a short trip to Nepal or have an interest in the Tharu culture then it **could well be interesting for you to visit**. ## Frequently Asked Questions about Tharu Village in Chitwan

Tharu Village showcases the indigenous Tharu people's culture in Chitwan National Park. Known for their unique mud houses, traditional dances, and festivals, it's an important site for understanding Nepal's Terai region's heritage and lifestyle. Tharu Village is near Sauraha, Chitwan's main gateway.

Join a guided tour (NPR 400), ox cart tour (NPR 1,200), pony cart tour (NPR 800), or walk/cycle independently (bicycle rental NPR 200). Entry is free; respect local customs by dressing modestly and asking permission for photos.

**Short answer: the Tharu Cultural Museum in Bachhauli, on the northern edge of Sauraha (Ratnanagar-07).**

It's the place to go for both things you asked about. The museum sits in the Tharu village of Bachhauli, about 800 m north-east of Sauraha's tourist strip — the nearest landmark cluster to the museum is the hamlet of Bachhauli itself, and the Sauraha suburb centre is roughly 570 m south-west of it. Inside, the collection displays the tools and traditional clothing the Tharu use in the fields, and the site includes a model/replica of a traditional Tharu home — the long mud-and-reed houses the community is known for. There's an entry fee.

A few practical notes from travelers:

- The village around the museum is a real, lived-in Tharu settlement of mud-and-reed huts, not a staged set. According to [The Longest Way Home](w4), it's about a 30–40 minute walk (roughly 2 km) from central Sauraha, flat and easy by bicycle (rentals around NPR 200 for a half day), and there's no charge to walk through the village itself — only the museum charges. The same guide notes the village's small museum displays field tools and traditional clothes, and that quiet independent visitors may even be invited in for tea.
- Guided half-day tours from Sauraha agents run about NPR 400 per person, or NPR 800–1,200 by pony or ox cart, but the village stop on those tours is brief.
- For seeing Tharu dress *worn* rather than displayed, the evening cultural dance programme in Sauraha is the complement: performers appear in black blouses and white saris, or white-and-red shirts with dhoti, as described by [Azure Sky Follows](w2). [The Longest Way Home](w1) notes the show runs nightly from about 7 pm and includes the peacock dance, and [Third Eye Traveller](w5) confirms the Tharu cultural house show is the standard evening activity in town.

So: museum in Bachhauli for the dress exhibits and replica house by day, the evening dance show in Sauraha for dress in performance.

**Coal Creek Falls** in the Coal Creek Scenic Reserve at Runanga, about 7 km northeast of Greymouth, is exactly the spot you're after.

  Cougar Mountain was extremely busy with coal mining from 1863-1963. The miners tunneled six miles under the mountain and strip mined the surface, eventually hauling out 11 million tons of bituminous coal. Remnants of the mining past are obvious when you see the large holes in the ground alongside the trail. These “cave holes” were formed when miner’s underground extractions got too close to the surface, which eventually led to cave-ins. Be sure to stay on the trail so as to avoid the deeper and potentially dangerous cave holes. One of the larger holes in the area is rumored to go 518 feet below sea level. Here's what I found for booking reindeer and husky safaris in Rovaniemi — there are both specialist farm operators and city-centre agencies that sell combined tours.

**Book direct with the operators**

- **Bearhill Husky** (Mykkälä, off Joulumaantie near Santa Claus Village) — the most frequently blogged husky kennel in the city, with 10 travel-blog mentions in the database and booking direct through its own site, bearhillhusky.com. A reviewer at [Dream Big Travel Far](w4) paid €129 per adult and €77 per child (ages 4–14), notes the price reflects higher animal-welfare standards, and adds that you can also book by phone on +358 (0)40 760 0020.
- **Raitola Reindeer & Husky Farm** (Välttikankaantie) — a single farm where you can do both a husky sled ride and a reindeer sleigh ride back to back. A traveler at [The Chic Advocate](w5) describes exactly that sequence: an energetic husky run followed by a quiet reindeer sleigh ride through the snow.
- **Santa Claus Reindeer** (Tähtikuja 1, at Santa Claus Village on the Arctic Circle) — the easiest one to reach without a transfer, and the reindeer half of most combination tours.
- **Konttaniemi Reindeer Farm** (Tamsintie 76) — a smaller reindeer farm with its own booking site, porofarmi.fi.

**Book through a city-centre agency**

- **Lapland Safaris** (Koskikatu 1, in the centre, about 450 m from the main street) — a full-service tour agency that sells the packaged safaris. If you'd rather have transport, winter gear and a guide bundled, this is the straightforward route.

**What the tours actually look like**

The classic product is the combined option: a 2.5-hour **Reindeer and Husky Safari** for people who can't choose between the two, as described by [Eternal Arrival](w3). There's also a longer 5-hour version that bundles snowmobiling with a reindeer ranch visit (feeding, optional sleigh ride) and a husky farm with a short sled ride — hotel pickup, thermal suits included — per [Megan Starr's tour roundup](w2). Her dog-sledding guide [w1] notes the same structure. One practical caveat from [Megan Starr](w2): the combined snowmobile-plus-animals tours pick up within about a 10 km radius of the centre, so confirm whether your accommodation is inside that zone before booking.

Quick tip: these two experiences are usually sold together because the reindeer farms and husky kennels sit in the same forest belt north of the city, so a single half-day works well. Book ahead in December–March, when the popular kennels sell out.

Here's what I found for booking reindeer and husky safaris in Rovaniemi — there are both specialist farm operators and city-centre agencies that sell combined tours.

**Book direct with the operators**

- **Bearhill Husky** (Mykkälä, off Joulumaantie near Santa Claus Village) — the most frequently blogged husky kennel in the city, with 10 travel-blog mentions in the database and booking direct through its own site, bearhillhusky.com. A reviewer at [Dream Big Travel Far](w4) paid €129 per adult and €77 per child (ages 4–14), notes the price reflects higher animal-welfare standards, and adds that you can also book by phone on +358 (0)40 760 0020.
- **Raitola Reindeer & Husky Farm** (Välttikankaantie) — a single farm where you can do both a husky sled ride and a reindeer sleigh ride back to back. A traveler at [The Chic Advocate](w5) describes exactly that sequence: an energetic husky run followed by a quiet reindeer sleigh ride through the snow.
- **Santa Claus Reindeer** (Tähtikuja 1, at Santa Claus Village on the Arctic Circle) — the easiest one to reach without a transfer, and the reindeer half of most combination tours.
- **Konttaniemi Reindeer Farm** (Tamsintie 76) — a smaller reindeer farm with its own booking site, porofarmi.fi.

**Book through a city-centre agency**

- **Lapland Safaris** (Koskikatu 1, in the centre, about 450 m from the main street) — a full-service tour agency that sells the packaged safaris. If you'd rather have transport, winter gear and a guide bundled, this is the straightforward route.

**What the tours actually look like**

The classic product is the combined option: a 2.5-hour **Reindeer and Husky Safari** for people who can't choose between the two, as described by [Eternal Arrival](w3). There's also a longer 5-hour version that bundles snowmobiling with a reindeer ranch visit (feeding, optional sleigh ride) and a husky farm with a short sled ride — hotel pickup, thermal suits included — per [Megan Starr's tour roundup](w2). Her dog-sledding guide [w1] notes the same structure. One practical caveat from [Megan Starr](w2): the combined snowmobile-plus-animals tours pick up within about a 10 km radius of the centre, so confirm whether your accommodation is inside that zone before booking.

Quick tip: these two experiences are usually sold together because the reindeer farms and husky kennels sit in the same forest belt north of the city, so a single half-day works well. Book ahead in December–March, when the popular kennels sell out.

The airport you're thinking of is **Telluride Regional Airport (TEX)**, in San Miguel County, Colorado, about six miles west of Telluride.

**Why it fits your description:** The field sits on a mesa high above the San Miguel River valley, with the runway ending at a sheer drop-off rather than flat overrun — pilots literally land on top of a cliff. One traveler who has flown both described Telluride as the only landing that rivaled Paro, saying you "land on the top of a cliff in the middle of the Rocky Mountains" ([My Travelling Circus](w1)). A visitor riding the free gondola over the plateau noted you never want to overshoot a runway, "but at Telluride you reaaaaaaaally don't want to overshoot" ([No Home Just Roam](w7)) — a good summary of the danger, since there's no gentle ground beyond the threshold.

**Practical notes:** The airport (ref W315390123, listed in the database at Terminal Departures And Arrivals, San Miguel) is high-altitude and weather-prone, so flights are limited and fares tend to be steep — many visitors instead fly into Montrose Regional Airport and shuttle the ~1.5 hours in ([Fearless Captivations](w9), [The World on My Necklace](w10)). If you want to combine the aviation-geek visit with sightseeing, Bridal Veil Falls (also in San Miguel County, just east of town) is one of the most-visited spots in the area.

For comparison, the other famous "cliff at the end of the runway" airport is Lukla in Nepal — but that one's runway slopes upward into a mountainside with a free-fall drop at the end, and it's not in the United States ([Earth Trekkers](w8)).

**Meany Lodge** is the place you're thinking of — the first ski resort in Washington, and it does feel like a time machine.

**What it is:** A rustic mountain hut/lodge run entirely by volunteers from The Mountaineers, with a rope tow that's essentially unchanged for a century. According to [Where is Kyle Miller?](w1), the building "was the first ski resort in Washington and it felt like a time machine walking through the front door," and the same page notes the lodge's lift system has stayed much the same over the last century — guests still grab a fast-moving rope tow, and everyone pitches in with chores from cooking to cleaning.

**Where it is:** Meany Lodge sits in Kittitas County, Washington, off **Forest Road 54** — in the Stampede Pass area east of Snoqualmie Pass, reached in winter by snowcat from the Stampede Pass parking lot (or on skis, as on the historic 20-mile Patrol Race from Snoqualmie West). Coordinates: 47.28033, -121.32029. It's listed in the database as a mountain hut with a Wikipedia entry and a Mountaineers page.

One clarification worth flagging: it's commonly described as a "Snoqualmie Pass" ski destination, but strictly speaking the lodge is a bit southeast of the pass summit, near Stampede Pass — not at the Summit at Snoqualmie ski area itself. If you were picturing the big resort complex on I-90, that's a different (much newer) operation.

[w1] Patrol Race: Snoqualmie to Meany Lodge Snoqualmie Pass Ski Tours Where is Kyle Miller?
The Patrol Race was one of the original ski tours within Washington State that dates back to the 1930’s. Its history comes from the original ski resort in the Cascades called Meany Lodge and started by the Mountaineers. The route itself starts at Snoqualmie West and follows the forests nearly 20 miles to Meany Lodge.

This was the first race of its kind in North America and ran until America’s involvement in WW2. Luckily it was started again in 2014 and I was in one of the groups to keep history alive.

This Trip would connect **Crystal Mountain to Stampede Pass** to the South and the **Alpine Lakes Traverse** to the North from **Mount Rainier** to **Mount Baker**. A few months earlier I had been invited by my friend Nigel Steere to be involved in the Patrol Race.

Not many people know it but the Pacific Northwest has a long history of mountaineering. Being a long time supporter of storytelling and keeping these legends alive I was honored to be involved.

in the race. I had become a Nordic Skiing Splitboarder. We were the last group in the staggered start and enjoyed easy navigation. By now the skin track was broken in by over 10 other groups as we made our way past Snoqualmie West. Breaking off of the summer trail we found ourselves on a snow covered groomer and making good time on the Patrol Race. As we made it through the Snoqualmie Pass Nordic area we broke off onto the Patrol Race trail. By now the snow was deep and we were thankful that others had broken in the trail the day before.

What took us 30 minutes to go through must have taken the original group hours. The weather was coming in and out as we made our way past open alpine slopes. Soon we would be on Forest Service Roads for the rest of the Patrol Race. Once it was time for our first descent we had a view of the terrain to our south. It was a mixture of clear cuts and spaced out forests. Zig Zagging through the area was the occasional road. It was a quiet day in the Snoqualmie Pass backcountry that would be broken by snowmobile engines. Skinning through the forests we were happy to find shelter from the strong winds. Looking in front of us it was east to spot where the wind was coming from. Each and every tree showed signs of how bad the weather was the previous few days. 20 Miles and countless hours later we arrived at Meany Lodge which was bustling with activity. This was a place I was always interested in seeing and it felt fitting to ski there from **Snoqulamie Pass**. The building was the first ski resort in Washington and it felt like a time machine walking through the front door.

The rest of the day we celebrated the Patrol Race event with the other groups. They handed out different awards for both speed and style as the day went on. It was great being a part of the small community for a day. That night we all had choirs from cleaning to cooking before it was time to go to bed. The next morning we woke up to new snow as they dug out the rope tow. Everyone there was a volunteer. They had a rule that if you were going to go ski you had to right what you were doing on the board. With the conditions being so good this was my one time to experience both the riding and the culture at Meany Lodge. Like the lodge the lift system was relatively unchanged over the last century and it was like looking at history. At the base there was a small building with an engine running the rope tow.

It was awesome to see and made me happy to think that at one time all the ski resorts in North America were like this. The hardest part of the trip was committing to grab onto the rope as it was going fast. Any hesitation would both destroy your gear and burn your hands.

There was no 90% commitment you were all in. Once you were holding on the rope would drag you up the hill. It was very similar to the **club field culture of New Zealand. **

The resort was small but the terrain, history and people really make the place special. For the next few hours I explored the terrain around Meany Lodge before heading on the snow cat down to the Stampede Pass parking lot. It was a great experience and you felt like you were a part of history doing. Thank you to Nigel Steere for putting the Patrol Race on and it was an honor being involved. **Click here to check out more of our trips from Mount Rainier to Mount Baker**

Thank you for reading this trip from Snoqualmie West to Meany Lodge via the Patrol Race. If you want to see more ski tours within the **Snoqualmie Pass Backcountry** check out this link.

**Meany Lodge** is the place you're thinking of — the first ski resort in Washington, and it does feel like a time machine.

**What it is:** A rustic mountain hut/lodge run entirely by volunteers from The Mountaineers, with a rope tow that's essentially unchanged for a century. According to [Where is Kyle Miller?](w1), the building "was the first ski resort in Washington and it felt like a time machine walking through the front door," and the same page notes the lodge's lift system has stayed much the same over the last century — guests still grab a fast-moving rope tow, and everyone pitches in with chores from cooking to cleaning.

**Where it is:** Meany Lodge sits in Kittitas County, Washington, off **Forest Road 54** — in the Stampede Pass area east of Snoqualmie Pass, reached in winter by snowcat from the Stampede Pass parking lot (or on skis, as on the historic 20-mile Patrol Race from Snoqualmie West). Coordinates: 47.28033, -121.32029. It's listed in the database as a mountain hut with a Wikipedia entry and a Mountaineers page.

One clarification worth flagging: it's commonly described as a "Snoqualmie Pass" ski destination, but strictly speaking the lodge is a bit southeast of the pass summit, near Stampede Pass — not at the Summit at Snoqualmie ski area itself. If you were picturing the big resort complex on I-90, that's a different (much newer) operation.

**Lanzarote** — the easternmost Canary Island, and the one where both the raw volcanic terrain and César Manrique's work are concentrated.

The lava fields come from the eruptions of 1730–1736 (and again in 1824), which buried a quarter of the island and left the surreal, near-lunar terrain now protected as **Timanfaya National Park** in the southwest, around the Montañas del Fuego. As [souvenirs.vincent.voyage](w2) puts it, roughly three-quarters of Lanzarote's surface is lava fields and arid volcanic landscape, and the 1730 eruption alone swallowed ten villages. The park's Ruta de los Volcanes and its geothermal demonstrations (bushes igniting, water shot back as steam) are the classic way to see it, per [The Travel Hack](w1).

Manrique, a Lanzarote native, built his signature "art fused into nature" installations right into that geology:

- **Jameos del Agua** — a collapsed lava tube in Haría turned into a cave auditorium, pool and restaurant (open Su–Fr 10:00–18:30, with "Jameos Nights" on Fridays).
- **Fundación César Manrique** in Tahíche — the artist's former home built over volcanic bubbles in the lava flow.
- **Casa-Museo César Manrique** in Haría — his later residence, open daily 10:30–18:00.
- **Restaurante El Diablo** inside Timanfaya, where he used the ground's own geothermal heat to grill — noted by [Eternal Arrival](w5).

So: Lanzarote, with Timanfaya as the lava-field heart and the Manrique sites scattered across the island.

  Designed by local artist César Manrique (yes, him again!) the garden is one of his most celebrated creations, seamlessly blending art with nature. Covering about 51 square kilometres, the park is renowned for its dramatic terrain, shaped by volcanic eruptions that occurred between 1730 and 1736, and again in 1824. These eruptions left a surreal landscape of lava fields, craters, and volcanic cones, giving the park a unique, almost lunar appearance. Timanfaya is home to the famous Montañas del Fuego (Fire Mountains), where geothermal activity is still visible today. # Hotel Review: Oasis Smart Cancun Hotel, Downtown Cancun

*Looking for an affordable adults-only hotel in Cancun? Check out the Oasis Smart Cancun Hotel for a relaxing stay away from the parties of the beachside resort! *

I don’t tend to post a whole heap of hotel reviews on here. Because usually, hotels to me are simply a place to lay my head between getting out there and exploring. Occasionally, I do stay in a hotel that’s worth talking about. My trip to Berlin saw me monkeying around in the 24Hours Hotel there; and I had an amazing experience staying at Pineapple Beach Club in Antigua. After my tour of the Yucatan Peninsula, I’d booked a couple of extra nights in Cancun to recharge a little before my flight. Cancun itself didn’t impress me much, to be honest – but the hotel I stayed in did. *Enter the  Oasis Smart Hotel in Downtown Cancun.

*

**Contents**show

*Posts on Mini Adventures use affiliate links. If you make a purchase through these links, I’ll earn a small commission which helps me keep this site alive (at no additional cost to you!)

*

## Finding a Hotel in Downtown Cancun

I wanted to find a hotel in downtown Cancun that wasn’t the hotel zone, because a) it was closer to the airport and b)

the effort of dealing with families and partygoers felt way too much…effort. I chose the Smart Cancun Hotel, because it was pretty cheap (about £45 per night), and looked nice on the internet, basically. The **Smart Cancun Hotel** is actually joined with the Oh! Cancun Hotel, both owned by Oasis but with rooms sold separately. If you’re thinking of booking the Oh! Cancun, it’s worth checking out the Oasis Smart instead. The rooms are of the same standard, the facilities all shared and rooms at the latter are often a bit cheaper.

## The Rooms

The rooms at the Smart Cancun aren’t anything mega fancy – but at the price, you wouldn’t expect them to be. But for how much I paid, it was certainly a very decent room. The HUGE bed was really comfy, and I spent both mornings there having a good ol’ lie in. The all-important bathroom toiletries situation impressed me too. Toothbrush and toothpaste were welcomed, and the sewing kit came in super handy when I managed to rip one of my favourite playsuits.

Also, there was a balcony. I barely used it other than for drying clothes, but it’s always good to have. My only gripe? The air con in the room was SUPER NOISY, and I couldn’t sleep with it on, which resulted in some slightly uncomfortable nights. **The Pool at Smart Cancun**

I have to say, it was the shots of the pool online that swayed me towards booking.

Palm trees, check. Sparkling blue water, check. Four poster poolside beds, check. Thankfully, the online pictures weren’t much different to how the pool area actually looked, which was a pleasant discovery. I arrived at around 4.30pm, and as soon as I’d checked in, it was straight down to the sunbeds with a book to make the most of the lovely weather before meeting friends for dinner. I spent the following two days basically not leaving the hotel, aside from a wander to a local market. I’m not usually the kinda gal who can sit in the sun doing nothing – but with a couple of charity shop reads, plentiful Pina Coladas and some good old factor 50, I was pretty much set. **Dining and Drinking** My booking included a breakfast buffet – but this wasn’t your standard, English sausage-and-eggs affair. There WERE scrambled eggs, but they featured chunks of chorizo and spring onions. Refried beans were a surprisingly very good addition to breakfast dishes, and for the more traditional, cold meats, cheeses, fruit and pastries were on offer too. Oh, and I drank A LOT of chocolate milk. On my second night at the hotel, I decided to be super lazy and order room service. Here’s a fact – I’d never actually ordered room service until this trip. *I KNOW*.

I ordered a tasty and generously sized dish of chicken fajitas, and a trio of gorgeous chocolate cakes. I ate it all in bed while watching Jack Whitehall’s stand up, drinking fizzy apple juice and feeling guilty when I spilt some hot sauce on my newly-changed crisp white sheets…

Fancy a drink?

The poolside White Terrace Bar is pretty well priced, and has a decent selection. There’s also the Red Hot Coyote Club if you fancy some evening entertainment – I didn’t actually go though (I prefer to spend my evenings in bed with Mr. Whitehall), so can’t comment on that one! **Kin-Ha Wellness Spa**

On my last afternoon, I decided to treat myself to a ‘Moonlight’ massage, beside the pool. It was definitely worth spending on – I felt like a total queen afterwards, as I sipped on my included glass of fizz. **Is Smart Cancun worth staying at?**

If you’re looking for a reasonably priced hotel in downtown Cancun, the Oasis Smart is definitely worth considering. You’ll find a decent pool area, comfortable rooms and a location that’s well situated for both local exploration and getting to the beach. Friendly staff and a colourful lobby create a welcoming atmosphere, and the included buffet breakfast is a definite plus point. **Tours & Activities in Cancun**

Truth or Consequences (locals call it "T or C") is a geothermal town on the Rio Grande, and its best-known soak is **Riverbend Hot Springs**, a riverside bathhouse on Austin Street with a handful of travel-blog mentions. Several other in-town facilities also let visitors soak in the thermal water:

One caveat: the "free" label comes from the travel write-ups rather than a price I could confirm on the company's own site, so I'd verify by phone before making a special trip.
