Here's what I found in Wynwood:

**Wood Tavern** — 2531 NW 2nd Avenue, right in the heart of Wynwood. This is the closest match to what you're describing: a locals' bar with a relaxed outdoor patio and a well-regarded happy hour, plus daily specials. It's open Tuesday–Saturday 5 pm–3 am and Sunday 3–11 pm, and it's connected to the Bar Next Door, which serves burgers right off the patio. According to [Adventures Around Skye](w1), it's the spot for "a cold beer at a locals' bar" with an awesome happy hour and relaxed patio vibe — and on the second Saturday of the month the Art Walk food trucks gather right there.

**Gramps** — on NW 24th Street, a few blocks north. A dive-bar-meets-cocktail-lounge with craft beers, pizza served in the garden out back at night, and a rotating lineup of bands, DJs, karaoke and trivia. [alexinwanderland](w3) calls it the perfect blend of dive bar, lounge cocktail list and brewery-level craft beer, and singles out its weekday happy hour from 4–7 pm as the reason it "would definitely be our local if we lived here."

One caveat: [sheiswanderlust](w4) also mentions **El Patio** as a Wynwood staple with a mostly open-air setup, but I could not confirm it in the places database — the only "El Patio" entries I found are hotels in Key West and Venice Beach, Florida, so I'd treat that recommendation as unverified.

For your criteria — relaxed patio plus good happy hour — Wood Tavern is the strongest pick, with Gramps a close second if you want better beer and a livelier evening scene.

With sharpened wooden poles and even a rake and hammer in hand, pedestrians are confronting the pesky salespeople – those with happy hour menus who try to woo passersby to imbibe at their street-side cafes and restaurants. “This is obviously a battle scene,” says Joe Furst with Goldman Properties, one of the companies involved with creating the Wynwood Walls. “If you’ve ever been to Ocean Drive, there are always these hawkers trying to get you to sit at their restaurants at happy hour with half price drinks.”

  ## Wynwood ### The Dirty Rabbit The Dirty Rabbit fits Wynwood perfectly, a casual, artsy and fun bar with a mix of DJs and themed nights. It’s smaller than the South Beach clubs but has a great vibe, with DJs playing everything from reggaeton to house. It’s a good place to start a night in Wynwood before moving to other spots. ### El Patio El Patio has become a staple in Wynwood for Latin music and dancing. The setup is mostly open-air, and people actually come here to dance, not just to stand around. They have a huge selection of all kinds of liquor at their bar. Its open-air design and casual atmosphere make it a popular choice for those looking for a less formal nightlife experience. ### ZeyZey ZeyZey is one of Wynwood’s newer venues, mixing live music, DJs, and cultural events. It is a cozy and intimate venue featuring an outdoor main stage and a smaller indoor space with a club-like vibe. It offers a more diverse lineup compared to traditional nightclubs, often highlighting international and local artists. The crowd is more mixed too, and you’ll often find international acts here that you might not see elsewhere in Miami. ## Brickell ### Blackbird Ordinary Blackbird is more of a bar than a nightclub, but it’s one of the most popular nightlife spots in Brickell. It has DJs, a big dance floor, and plenty of space to just hang out with friends. It’s a popular option among locals and offers a different vibe from Miami’s larger clubs.

For top-quality gelato right in Kotor's Old Town, my pick is **Moritz Eis** — a small Balkan chain that travelers rate as the best ice cream in town despite the higher prices. [Man Vs Globe](w2) admits they'd normally avoid recommending a chain over a local independent, but says Moritz's gelato "was good enough to shout about," with unusual flavors like lemon-basil sorbet, rhubarb and ginger, and baked peach alongside classics. There are several branches in Montenegro, with two inside Kotor's Old Town: the one at 495 Stari Grad (open 09:00–24:00) and another on Pjaca Škaljarska square. There's also a smaller "Moritz" spot on Pjaca od Oružja with shorter hours (11:00–19:00).

If you want the local artisan alternative, the other shop that keeps coming up is **Marshall's Gelato**, praised for its pistachio in particular by [Where Goes Rose](w4) and [mybibimbaplife](w3) — one writer paid €3 for a pistachio cone and chatted with the passionate owner. However, I have to flag this honestly: I could not resolve Marshall's in the places database, so I can't give you a verified location or ref for it — the name appears in travel writing but not in the mapping data I can search. Moritz Eis is the one I can confirm is physically in the Old Town.

Bottom line: go to Moritz Eis at 495 Stari Grad for reliable, high-quality (and yes, pricier) gelato, and keep an eye out for Marshall's signage if you want to try the pistachio the bloggers rave about.

[w2] Where to Eat and Drink Around Kotor Bay: The 10 Best Restaurants - Man Vs Globe
Recessing inland from Montenegro’s sun kissed Adriatic coast, the Bay of Kotor is a tourist draw thanks to charming towns that are brimming with rich history, its tranquil waters, and the breathtaking mountainous backdrop.

Alongside all of these delights, it’s also a haven for foodies. Cuisine in the region is mostly influenced by the body of water that sits at its centre; You will find fresh seafood on most menus, caught the same day by the fleets of small vessels that embark on the journey through the mouth of the bay and out into the Mediterranean in search of octopus, squid and tuna that is often cooked and served in a simple, fuss-free manner. At the same time, Montenegrin food is one that draws influences from surrounding regions. It’s a melting pot of cultural influences ranging from Italian and Balkan to Croatian and Greek. While pasta and pizza feature heavily on menus, borrowing from their neighbours across the Adriatic – often featuring locally sourced shrimp, mussels and clams – so do meat-heavy traditional dishes from Serbia and Albania such as cevapcici, pljeskavice, raznjici, as well as Montenegro’s own famous Njegusi sausage. ## Where to Eat and Drink Around Kotor Bay

It’s been a long time since Kotor has been considered a hidden gem or off-the-beaten-path destination.

Its UNESCO World Heritage status has brought the crowds. Now, multiple enormous cruise ships drop their anchor in the bay each day, packing the old town with tourists and increasing the number of disappointing tourist trap restaurants that have popped up to capitalise on Montenegro’s new-found popularity. That isn’t to say that there aren’t some truly wonderful dining experiences to be found in Kotor itself. The Old Town is dotted with picturesque and atmospheric little squares that can provide and tranquil al fresco dining experience in an evening once the cruise-goers have made their way back to their cabins. While some of the places that line the squares pump out over-priced, low-quality food, there are gems to be found amongst them, especially if you choose to head down the narrow, winding backstreets. However, some of the best gastronomic experiences are found outside of the city itself. Smaller towns and villages play host to some fantastic family-run tavernas, all utilising produce from the hills and countryside that surround the bay as well as local cheeses, bread and cured meats. This list below is in no way extensive, but it represents a selection of the region’s finest restaurants and bars for anyone looking to avoid a disappointing meal.

### Konoba Scala Santa, Kotor

Picture the scene: The sun is setting, bathing the stone buildings of Kotor’s old town in glowing orange hues. You’re sat in a quiet, atmospheric square, a glass of local wine in hand while people mill around.

A busker entertains passers-by with traditional Montenegrin songs on his accordion and laughing kids frolic in the plaza’s water fountain. This is what I experienced while dining at Scala Santa which seems like a perfectly quaint ambience in which to be enjoying Kotor’s oldest restaurant. The restaurant first opened its doors in 1931 and still oozes the same century-old charm thanks to its authentic interior, open fireplace and wooden beams that cross its low ceiling. This is very much a traditional tavern and a perfect escape from the bustle of the Old Town. However, if you do want to be in the midst of the action, Scala Santa’s large terrace spills out into the plaza and is the perfect place to sit with an aperitif or enjoy your meal later into the evening. Like most restaurants in the country, the menu is packed with pasta, seafood, and typical fish dishes all giving a sense of home cooking, particularly the fish stew that the restaurant is most well-known for. I opted to give the seafood a miss, after a week of eating nothing but fish. Instead, I decided to devour the spicy beef pasta and certainly wasn’t disappointed.

**Where:** 85330 Trg od Salate, Kotor**When:** Daily 10am – 10pm

### Konoba Škver, Herceg Novi

Often called ‘The City of the Sun’ thanks to the large number of sunny days it experiences throughout the year, the town of Herceg Novi sits at the mouth of the Bay of Kotor, its fortresses and steps cascading down a steep hillside and leading to its harbour. It’s this connection to the sea and the bay that defines much of the menus in the town, with seafood in abundance. One restaurant in particular is famed for its fish, squid and octopus – Konoba Škver. The owner of Konoba Škver is a keen tuna fisherman, often heading out on his boat in the morning to seek a fresh catch that he can serve to diners. However, the restaurant is also known for its wonderful, traditional seafood risottos, both shrimp and saffron or a traditional black risotto dish. On top of the wonderful food, the setting adds to the atmosphere. The restaurant sits right beside the water, with views of the harbour and small boats bobbing on the waves just a few feet away. **Where:** 42 Pet Danica Walkway, Herceg Novi**When:** Daily 12pm – 11.30pm

### Restaurant Conte, Perast

Possibly the most alluring town that sits on the shores of the Bay of Kotor, Perast was once rich and powerful, as seen in the fact that this small settlement contains 16 churches and 17 sprawling palaces (most of which are now home to restaurants and hotels). This is all despite only having one street, which curves along the waterfront and is buzzing with tourists, bars and dining spots.

These waterfront terraces are beautiful spaces to spend the evening gorging on local cuisine while looking out at the two islands that sit in the bay a short distance from the shore: Gospa of Škrpjela – an island that was artificially created in 1452 around a rock where locals discovered an image of the Madonna, eventually building a church in the 17th century – and Sveti Djordje, which houses a Benedictine Monastery and is said to be cursed.

Thankfully, Hotel Conte has a less sinister reputation. Sitting within a palace that was lovingly restored by the Kasalica family and transformed into the Conte Hotel and Restaurant. The buildings have been modernised while taking care to preserve their original character, indigenous architecture and historical elements and the restaurant aims to revive old Montenegrin recipes using fresh. local ingredients, such as Montenegrin fish, red shrimps from Albania, oysters from Mali Ston, and Kvarner shrimps.

**Where:** bb Ul. Marka Martinovića, Perast **When:** Daily 8am – 12am

### Ćatovića Mlini, Morinj

You only have to look at the wall of luminaries that adorns the wall of Ćatovića Mlini to see its place in the Montenegrin culinary scene: A photographic who’s who of the nation’s celebrities alongside international stars such as Novak Djokovic, Gerard Butler, and strangely, Bruce Forsyth, who have all chosen to dine here. Meaning ‘the Catovic’s Mills’, Catovica Mlini is where the Catovic family has used their mills for over two centuries to make flour. In the last 25 years, the latest owner Lazar and his family have worked lovingly to turn the former mill buildings into one of Montenegro’s best restaurants. This gives it an idyllic countryside setting, just inland from the small coastal village of Morinj, halfway between the larger settlements of Herceg Novi and Kotor. The romantic old stone mills are still there, along with the water wheel and the stream that serves it.

Geese and peacocks wander around the luscious, mountain-backed grounds, and the soothing sound of babbling waterways creates a tranquil atmosphere. Dining here feels like you are in the remote countryside, despite only being a few minutes from the busy coastline of Boka Bay. It isn’t just the location that makes Catovica Mlini so appealing. The menu is the main draw, packed with traditional Njegusi specialities made from locally sourced ingredients giving a farm-to-fork dining experience paired with some of the finest local wines. We opted for a 5-course tasting menu with a wine pairing that offered octopus, a mixed seafood platter, and seabass on black rice with a white truffle sauce that was absolutely delectable.

**Where:** E65, Morinj 85338**When:** Daily 12pm – 9pm

### Kraken Underwater Wine Cellar

Anyone who has travelled to Montenegro will be aware of the country’s rich winemaking traditions. Still, the people behind Kraken Wine Cellar have elevated this heritage by harnessing the power of the sea to create a revolutionary approach to winemaking. Inspired by tales of shipwrecks found to contain centuries-old bottles of wine that have been perfectly preserved, the Kraken team decided to place 200 bottles at the bottom of the sea, intrigued by the possibility of enhancing the ageing process using the sea’s natural elements. After salvaging their bounty a year later, they found that the process had worked – the wine was more refined. Although this may sound like a bit of a gimmick, it’s thought that the constant pressure, temperature, absence of light and noise, along with gentle constant currents are all beneficial for ageing wine using this method. You can sample these wines by taking a tender out to Kraken’s cool pontoon wine bar, floating out in the bay between Orahovac and Perast. Here you can indulge in delectable fresh seafood while sipping this unique wine in a rather distinctive setting. They also offer visits to the wine bar as part of their boat tours around the bay.

**Where:** Dražin Vrt 85330

### Lighthouse Restaurant and OLE! Beach & Bar, Hyatt Regency Kotor

Nestled beside the waters of Boka Bay, within a short drive of both Tivat and the charming old town of Kotor, the tranquil Hyatt Regency Kotor Bay Resort offers one of the most luxurious stays to be found in Montenegro. The hotel’s on-site restaurants are no different. Accessible by boat via the hotel’s private marina, The Lighthouse Restaurant offers an ever-evolving à la carte menu of seasonal Mediterranean cuisine with an Adriatic Sea backdrop surrounded by the Bay’s stunning fjord Landscape. For a more casual dining experience, the beachfront Olé! Beach and Bar dishes out exotic cocktails and Latin specialities such as tacos ceviche just metres from the water’s edge, all to the upbeat sounds of salsa and Latino rhythms.

**Where:** Hyatt Regency Kotor Bay Resort, Donji Stoliv bb, 85330 ** When:** Daily 12pm – 12am

### Rooftop Terrace Hippocampus, Kotor

Located inside of a centuries-old building in the centre of Kotor’s old town, Boutique Hotel Hippocampus Is one of the city’s most stylish and romantic places to stay. Even if you don’t have a room of your own, you can drop in to experience the hotel’s roof terrace which offers wonderful views over the nearby red-tiled roofs and church spires while sipping your freshly made cocktail. I only stopped in for a drink and didn’t get to sample the food, but I hear that they also have a fantastic menu of Mediterranean cuisine.

**Where:** Hotel Hippocampus, Old Town 489, Kotor**When:** Daily 9am – 11pm

### Moritz Eis, Kotor

The question of which shop serves the best Ice Cream in Kotor is hard-fought, with so many establishments vying for the money of sweltering tourists. I wouldn’t normally recommend a chain, instead opting for a local, independent spot.

However, the gelato from Moritz Eis was good enough to shout about. They have 9 stores in Montenegro, 2 of which are in Kotor while the others are in Tivat, Perast, Budva and Herceg Novi. All of these serve the same flavours which range from traditional tastes such as chocolate, berries or salted caramel, to the more interesting rhubarb and ginger or baked peach and vanilla. I chose to give my tastebuds a challenge and sample the lemon and basil sorbet, which is as delicious as it sounds.

**Where:* * 293 Pjaca od salate, Kotor**When:** Daily 9am – 10pm

### BBQ Tanjga, Kotor

For top-quality gelato right in Kotor's Old Town, my pick is **Moritz Eis** — a small Balkan chain that travelers rate as the best ice cream in town despite the higher prices. Bottom line: go to Moritz Eis at 495 Stari Grad for reliable, high-quality (and yes, pricier) gelato, and keep an eye out for Marshall's signage if you want to try the pistachio the bloggers rave about.

[w1] Visitor's Guide To Phipps Conservatory, Pittsburgh's Botanical Garden Jewel - The Geographical Cure
If you’re planning a trip to Pittsburgh, don’t miss the opportunity to include the exquisite Phipps Conservatory in your bucket list or itinerary. Nestled within the picturesque Schenley Park in the Oakland neighborhood, Phipps Conservatory is a serene oasis of botanical beauty. Renowned as one of Pittsburgh’s premier attractions, Phipps boasts an astonishing array of lush floral collections, intricate glass artistry, and captivating themed exhibits. Wander through its peaceful landscapes, where each step reveals a vibrant tapestry of plants from around the world. The conservatory’s harmonious blend of nature and artistry creates an enchanting ambiance that’s perfect for relaxation and exploration. From the moment you enter, you’ll be greeted by a symphony of colors, scents, and textures. Phipps Conservatory is more than just a garden. It’s a captivating journey through the wonders of the natural world. Whether you’re a botany enthusiast, an art lover, or simply seeking a tranquil escape, Phipps Conservatory offers a unique experience that will leave you inspired and refreshed. Opened in 1893, Phipps Conservatory was created by philanthropist and Carnegie Steel co-founder Henry W. Phipps. He sought to create a source of learning and enjoyment for the citizens of Pittsburgh. Phipps was a botany enthusiastic who gifted his creation to the city. Phipps Conservatory is one of the few remaining public gardens that still produces full scale season flower shows year round. The glass, stone, and steel building is dubbed the “crystal palace.” Glass panes cover nearly 100% of the facade. **Overview Of Phipps Conservatory**

If you’re on a budget, the outdoor gardens are completely free. On one side (toward the University of Pittsburgh campus), you’ll find an enchanted garden with all manner of perennials, trees, ferns, and a pond. On the other side, opposite the main entrance, you’ll find the aquatic garden.

It’s filled with water lilies and guarded by a Neptune statue. Inside, the Victorian greenhouse has a wide ranging collection of 14 indoor gardens. The well manicured exhibits range from miniature orchids to massive palm trees, with astonishing attention to detail in each room. In addition to the permanent displays, Phipps has temporary themed exhibits and exhibits celebrating each season. This makes Phipps a great place for repeat visits. As a local, I go about twice a year. I recently visited for Fall Flower Show, which was titled *The Poetry of Nature*. It featured an extravagant showing of mums (13 types), asters, coleus, hydrangea, willows, and other glowing plants.

Having been dazzled by that, I returned for the __ Winter Fl____ower__ __ Sho____w at Christmas__. I’ve even attended at wedding at Phipps. **Guide To Phipps Conservatory**: **What To See**

On a visit to Phipps Conservatory, you enter through a beautiful lobby in the crystal palace. You’re greeted by a gorgeous pendant glass chandelier, *Goldenrod, Teal and Citron*, in the lobby. It was crafted by renowned Seattle glass artist __

Dale Chihuly__. In fact, there quite a few of his pieces in the museum, beautifully tucked among the plants. They almost seem alive with their sinuous lines. The forms and colors of the glass imitate, and blissfully coexist, with the plant growth.

When you enter the building, there’s a map showing all the main rooms. There’s also signage in each room explaining what’s there. You can follow the designated path throughout the exhibit rooms, constantly moving to the right, or do your own thing. Each room has a theme dedicated to a region or specific type of plant. All the rooms are incredible, but these were my favorites. You start your visit in the famed Palm Court, which serves as the grand entrance to the rest of the indoor displays. This historic glass house features many different species of palm trees. The sun casting a beautiful light on the plants.

It also boasts two beautiful Chihuly sculptures, *Paintbrushes* and *Maccia Bowls*. One of my favorite rooms was the Frank Sarris Orchid Room, containing a magnificent array of beautiful orchids in different shades. You’ll also find the renowned Barbara Tisherman Slipper Orchid Collection. The rare lady slipper orchid is known for its unique bottom petal that resembles miniature footwear.

The Sunken Garden Room is truly peaceful. You almost wish you could sit down and read a book there. For the Fall Flower Show, there were velvety purple Mexican sage bushes everywhere

In the Serpentine Room, you’ll find a delightful collection of bonsai plants, some 40-60 years old. Bonsai means “tray planting” in Japanese. I especially liked the slanted bonsai that resembled wind swept trees. You’ll also find silverberries, weeping figs, natal plums, and chinese elm. In the Desert Room, the collection focuses on hot desert plants of the world. If you go gaga for agave or are a sucker for succulents, this room’s for you. There’s a beautiful Joshua Tree native to the Mojave Desert, saguaros, palo verde, fire barrels, aloe, and agave. The largest was an absolutely massive century plant.

The room is crowned with a spectacular yellow Chihuly chandelier, called *Desert Gold Star*. The Native Plants Room had scorchingly beautiful purple asters on display. I also saw purple hyssop, purple skullcaps, bearberry, and bayberry. The Broderie Room is also quite beautiful as well, featuring formal French Louis XIV style gardens. It’s known as the Parterre de Broderie, which translates to “embroidery of the earth.”

This romantic room is a popular setting for weddings in Pittsburgh. This year, the room was filled with gorgeous shades of pink and purple mums and asters. At the back of the Broderie Room are four bronze statues, created by Edmond Amateis and gifted to Phipps by the Mellon Estate.

One of the most stunning gardens is the Tropical Forest Conservatory. It’s quite grand (60 feet tall). The room is topped with a crystal dome and set out in winding pathways. There are also hanging lights, waterfalls, a treehouse, a gazebo, and a fish pond. This room features a different region of the world every three years.

On this visit, the focus was on Cuba. Cuba’s ecosystems are thriving right now, likely from a lack of tourism. Many scientists want to do research in Cuba because of its biodiversity and unspoiled wild places. The Fruits and Spices Room showcases exotic varieties. Among other things, you’ll find bright red miracle fruit, prickly lychees, prickly apple, and dragon fruit. This room also has a lovely Chihuly piece called *Celadon and Gilded Royal Purple Fiori*.

The Outdoor and Discovery Gardens are a peaceful haven. There are towering English oaks and beech trees. The borders were lined with huge hydrangeas. Bush clover nestled in the rocks. And tall willows wafted in the breeze. The Phipps campus also houses some of the most energy efficient environments in the world. Its Center for Sustainable Landscapes (CSL) is the first and only building to achieve four of the highest green building certifications. Phipps’ newest addition, the green Exhibit Staging Center (ESC), generates its own energy. It repurposes a former public works facility to be net-positive energy and net-zero water.

This is where Phipps creates its props and staging displays. You can see future flower shows in the making. Phipps also has a lovely gift shop with books, plant related items, home decor pieces, and a children’s section. The Phipps Cafe is touted as one of the best museum cafes in the United States, serving up local organic foods. And, indeed, I had a delicious mediterranean chicken wrap to conclude my visit.

**Practical Guide & Tips for Visiting Phipps Conservatory**

**Address**: 1 Schenley Park, Pittsburgh PA 15213

**Hours**: Open daily 9:30 am to 8:00 pm

**Entry fee**: $19.95 adults, seniors $17.95, $11.95 children 2-18, under 2 free

**Pro tip**: You’ll probably need about 90 minutes to see everything in a relaxed way. Try to visit on a Monday or Tuesday, as those are the least crowded days. No backpacks are allowed.

**Parking**: 

There is free parking for Phipps at the center island on Schenley Drive. If this is full, which it well might be, there is plenty of metered parking nearby. If you are there for an event, there will be valet parking. **Virtual Tour**:

**Hierba Dulce** in Oaxaca City is exactly what you're describing.

It's an all-vegan restaurant in the Barrio Mágico de Jalatlaco (Calle del General Porfirio Díaz, 68070), and it's the one place that matches all three of your criteria. According to [Pure Wander](w2), women-run establishments are a point of pride in Oaxaca, and Hierba Dulce is singled out as the standout: its all-vegan menu highlights many traditional styles of cooking, and the kitchen prides itself on using hyper-local ingredients specifically to push back against the over-industrialization of agriculture. The same piece recommends eating in the sunny courtyard and not skipping the homemade mole and fresh salsas.

[Your Friend the Nomad](w1) backs this up from the food angle — it describes Hierba Dulce as a widely popular organic, fully vegan restaurant serving traditional Oaxacan cuisine, loved by vegans and non-vegans, tourists and locals alike. A nice detail: a local (non-vegan) tour guide called it his favourite restaurant in Oaxaca because it's the only place making traditional dishes the way he grew up eating them in an Oaxacan village. That's a strong signal that the "traditional cooking" claim is real rather than marketing.

A couple of practical notes: the database entry has no opening hours on file, so it's worth checking ahead or just turning up around a normal Oaxacan mealtime. If you want a second vegan option nearby, Herbívora (Calle de Tinoco y Palacios) is about 400 m from the centre and also fully vegan, though it's a more modern Mexican-vegan spot rather than a traditional-cooking project.

It's a small, beloved breakfast spot at 4935 Main Street (about 250 m from the village center), and it's exactly what you described: the local guide at [Where Are Those Morgans](w4) describes it as a "quaint diner serving pancakes, eggs and breakfast options," listing it among the top places to eat in Manchester Center. Travelers back this up — one blogger stopped in for coffee plus zucchini-bread French toast, a western omelet and turkey hash with poached eggs, arriving at 8:45 and finding a long line already forming by 9:15 ([Lyssy in the City](w1)). Another writer warns that it's popular enough that you may want to plan ahead, having missed out on a table there herself ([Blogger at Large](w3)).

Practical details from the database:
- **Address:** 4935 Main Street, Manchester Center, VT 05255
- **Phone:** +1-802-362-4204 — website upforbreakfastvt.com
- **Hours:** Monday–Friday 7:00 am–12:30 pm; Saturday–Sunday 7:00 am–1:30 pm (breakfast only, so get there early)
- **Note:** listed as not wheelchair accessible

If you'd rather have pancakes in a cushier setting, the Wilburton Inn up the road serves made-to-order breakfast with chocolate pancakes and Vermont maple syrup ([Wandering Wagars](w5)), but for a cozy village diner, Up for Breakfast is the match.

**Coronado Beach, right in front of the Hotel del Coronado, is the spot.** It's the one stretch of sand in Coronado that faces due west across the Pacific, so you get an unobstructed horizon with no land in the way — and the hotel's red turrets and the sand dunes give you a foreground. [Adventures n Sunsets](w1) singles out the Hotel del Coronado as having "its very own perfectly west-facing beach," and recommends walking from the hotel onto Coronado Beach for the sunset itself. [X Days In Y](w2) agrees, noting Coronado Beach "did not disappoint" and advising you arrive about 30 minutes before the sun goes down, since that's when the color show starts.

A few practical notes from the database:

- **Coronado Beach** (W233833244) is the main beach, about 400 m southwest of the Orange Avenue shops — the widest, most open sand.
- **Central Beach** (N358845839) is the adjacent section just south, in front of the Hotel del Coronado (R1785615), which is the most photographed angle. The hotel is the single most blogged-about place in town, so expect company at golden hour.
- **Sunset Park** (W233833243) in Coronado is a small inland neighbourhood park — despite the name, it has no ocean view, so don't be misled by it.
- **Centennial Park / Coronado Ferry Landing** (W44501644) on the bay side is lovely in the evening, but it faces *east* toward the San Diego skyline, so the sun sets behind you there. It's a good spot for the afterglow and city lights, not the sunset itself.

If you want the sun dropping into the water, head to the sand west of the Hotel del. If you want the skyline glowing pink, the Ferry Landing is the alternative.

**Coronado Beach, right in front of the Hotel del Coronado, is the spot.** It's the one stretch of sand in Coronado that faces due west across the Pacific, so you get an unobstructed horizon with no land in the way — and the hotel's red turrets and the sand dunes give you a foreground. [Adventures n Sunsets](w1) singles out the Hotel del Coronado as having "its very own perfectly west-facing beach," and recommends walking from the hotel onto Coronado Beach for the sunset itself. [X Days In Y](w2) agrees, noting Coronado Beach "did not disappoint" and advising you arrive about 30 minutes before the sun goes down, since that's when the color show starts.

A few practical notes from the database:

- **Coronado Beach** (W233833244) is the main beach, about 400 m southwest of the Orange Avenue shops — the widest, most open sand.
- **Central Beach** (N358845839) is the adjacent section just south, in front of the Hotel del Coronado (R1785615), which is the most photographed angle. The hotel is the single most blogged-about place in town, so expect company at golden hour.
- **Sunset Park** (W233833243) in Coronado is a small inland neighbourhood park — despite the name, it has no ocean view, so don't be misled by it.
- **Centennial Park / Coronado Ferry Landing** (W44501644) on the bay side is lovely in the evening, but it faces *east* toward the San Diego skyline, so the sun sets behind you there. It's a good spot for the afterglow and city lights, not the sunset itself.

If you want the sun dropping into the water, head to the sand west of the Hotel del. If you want the skyline glowing pink, the Ferry Landing is the alternative.

Based on my research, here's my recommendation:

## Top pick: Redstone Inn (Moab)

The **Redstone Inn** on Main Street is your best match. Travel writer Jess of [Im Jess Traveling](w1) calls it simply "the best place to stay in Moab on a budget" — a quaint, simple motel a few blocks south of downtown where every room has an efficiency kitchen, which helps keep food costs down. There's a hot tub, BBQ area, laundry and bike maintenance area on site, plus free pool access next door at its sister property, the Big Horn Lodge. Rate-wise, budget rooms in Moab generally start around $150/night per [a separate Moab budget guide](w1), making it far gentler on the wallet than the luxury properties like Hoodoo Moab or Sorrel River Ranch — and the red-rock name and setting fit your "warm tones and natural elements" brief nicely. Reachable at moabredstone.com / +1 435 259 3500.

## Budget-friendly alternative: Adventure Inn

If you want something on the north end of downtown (closer to Arches National Park), the **Adventure Inn** is an older but well-kept, solar-powered motel that [Im Jess Traveling](w1) rates as more affordable, walkable to several restaurants, with coffee machines, microwaves and A/C in every room. One caveat: another traveler noted these older motels "show their age" ([xdaysiny](w4)), so expect character over polish.

## Also worth knowing
- **Bowen Motel** — an affordable motel right on Main Street, with doubles around $186/night ([globetrottergirls](w2)).
- For an actual cozy, natural-materials vibe, [Eternal Arrival](w3) highlights **Bogie's Bungalow**, a budget downtown rental with "old-school wooden design, relaxing color scheme and exposure to natural light" — but that's an Airbnb, not a motel.

**My call:** go with the Redstone Inn for the best cozy-to-price ratio; pick Adventure Inn if you'd rather be closer to Arches.

## What I found

Your starting point is **Bowl and Pitcher Campground** (ref R5849951), on North Aubrey L White Parkway — the day-use area with flush toilets and campground showers, and the most commonly used Trail 25 start.

The key fact for your shuttle plan: **Trail 25** is the long spine route here — roughly a 25-mile loop on the west side of the Spokane River, and per [Washington Trails Association](w4) it "passes through or close to numerous trailhead parking access sites," which is exactly what makes it shuttle-friendly. WTA names the trailheads with easy access to Trail 25 as: **Equestrian, Morin, Marchand, the ORV area, Pine Bluff, Pine Bluff Road, Carlson, Deep Creek, McLellan Overlook, Seven Mile, and Wilber**.

**Trailheads I could confirm in the places database:**

- **Morin Trailhead** (ref W404682845) — on Equestrian Lane, about 575 m west of Bowl and Pitcher. This is the closest alternative trailhead to your start, essentially the "Equestrian" access on the WTA list.
- **Deep Creek Trailhead** (ref W396488316) — on North State Park Drive, up in the northwest part of the park near the Deep Creek overlook and Pine Bluff cliffs. This is the far end of the park from you, so it's a realistic shuttle target if you want a long one-way traverse.
- **Sontag Park trailhead** (ref W397728146) — a parking lot on West Charles Road in Nine Mile Falls, near the park's north edge. Note this one is *not* on WTA's Trail 25 list, so treat it as a nearby parking option rather than a confirmed Trail 25 access point.

**What I could not verify:** Marchand, the ORV area, Pine Bluff Road, Carlson, McLellan Overlook, Seven Mile, and Wilber trailheads did not come back as resolved entries in the places database, so I can't give you coordinates or refs for them. They're named by WTA as Trail 25 access points, but you'd want to confirm their exact locations with the park office or a current park map before committing a shuttle driver to them.

**Practical note:** Riverside State Park requires a Discover Pass, and per [adventuresofaplusk](w5) it's $46.99 for the annual pass and covers everyone in the car — worth buying in advance if you're leaving a vehicle at a second trailhead.

  The 2.1-mile Bowl & Pitcher loop in Riverside State Park, Spokane, features a CCC-built swinging bridge, Spokane River rapids, and basalt formations.
  This short hike boasts a lot of bang for your buck. At just 2.1 miles, the loop won't take too long, but you'll enjoy expansive views of an impressive river and rocky outcroppings. Start out by hiking across a swinging bridge at Bowl & Pitcher. This impressive bridge was built — like so many trail structures in the Spokane area — by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC). From the bridge, you can see large basalt structures rising out of the river as you cross into Riverside State Park. **The Neretva.**

Mostar is built astride the Neretva, the river that runs through the city's ravine — and it's the river the town's emblematic bridge spans. In the places database the Neretva resolves as a river feature just north-east of the centre ([Neretva](R2090864)), with the river continuing south toward Čapljina ([Neretva](W1191337316)). The bridge itself resolves as [Stari most](W444333266) (the "Old Bridge", in the Stari Grad quarter), a much-written-about landmark.

The day-trip connection you mention holds up in travel writing: several guides describe the Split–Mostar excursion as a cross-border trip to see the Ottoman-era old town and the bridge over the river. [Helena Bradbury](w1) notes that the smaller Kriva Ćuprija ("Crooked Bridge") also crosses the Neretva, while [Gina On A Plane](w4) frames the trip around cobbled streets, bazaars and "dramatic river views," and [Jess Bergin](w3) describes the Old Bridge joining two medieval towers across the water — where divers still leap off. [Brown Eyed Flower Child](w2) adds the practical details: roughly a two-hour drive from Split, with the Old Town market (Čaršija) and Stari Most as the highlights.

Good to know: it's a different country — Bosnia and Herzegovina — so bring your passport, as the guides above all stress.

rows.final:
**Short answer: treat it as an out-and-back side trip from the confluence, done without your pack.**

Here's how it works in practice:

- From the [White House Trailhead](N6404659104) you walk down the Paria riverbed; the canyon tightens into the Narrows around mile 4, and you hit the [Buckskin Gulch & Paria River Confluence](N1458539830) at roughly mile 7 — a very reasonable Day 1 if you're camping, and the usual lunch/rest point if you're pushing through.
- At the junction, turn **right (north/upstream)** into Buckskin rather than continuing down the Paria. Drop your pack at the confluence — there are established campsites on the sand and on the elevated ramp just above the junction, which is the first safe camp coming down Buckskin.
- The honest expectation: this is a *taste*, not a tour. [Bearfoot Theory](w3) describes spending about 20 minutes walking up Buckskin before the water got too deep — and Buckskin's pools are deeper and muckier than the Paria's. Budget 30–45 minutes round trip and accept that you'll stop at the first chest-deep pool.
- One obstacle to know about: just above the confluence there's a short 15–20 ft downclimb with a fixed rope and shallow moqui steps cut into the rock, which [Halfway Anywhere](w2) flags as insecure and awkward — especially with a pack or a dog. Going upstream you'll meet it head-on, so if it looks bad, that's your turnaround point. Leaving the pack behind is what makes this safe and quick.
- Two cautions. First, [Bearfoot Theory](w3) notes flash-flood risk peaks July–early September and the Narrows has stretches with no high ground — a side trip into an even tighter slot on a marginal weather day isn't worth it. Second, if you truly want Buckskin, the superior version is to descend the whole gulch from Wire Pass and exit via White House, as [365atlantatraveler](w4) outlines; a confluence side trip is a sampler.

So: reach the confluence on Day 1, stash your pack, walk up Buckskin for 15–30 minutes until the water or the rope climb stops you, then come back and camp at the junction before continuing down the Paria to White House.

[w1] 10 Best Utah Backpacking Trips – Bearfoot Theory
  Hiking the Paria River slot canyon from the White House trailhead, including a side trip into Buckskin Gulch, in the Paria Canyon-Vermilion Cliffs Wilderness Area.
  After leaving from the White House trailhead, the canyon begins narrowing down into its legendary slot, passing between towering red walls of Navajo sandstone. Just after 7 miles, you’ll pass the confluence with Buckskin Gulch with a few campsites near the junction. A side trip up the narrow corridor of Buckskin Gulch is a must-do. This is one of the most beautiful and harrowing slot canyons on Earth! Back in the Paria, you’ll continue south, following the endless twists, turns, and meanders into the ever-deepening and narrowing slot.
[w2] Buckskin Gulch and Paria Canyon – The Ultimate Backpacking Guide | HA
  Hiking the final stretch of Buckskin Gulch to the Paria River Confluence, identifying the first safe campsite, and transitioning into Paria Canyon toward Lees Ferry.
  From here, it's more of the same until just before reaching the **Paria River Confluence**. The canyon will open up significantly, revealing extensive vegetation on the left. You'll also find a sandy hill/ramp/elevated spot that you can hike to the top of. This is the **first safe campsite** encountered when hiking through Buckskin Gulch. There is space for camping up top and a few more spots lower down. I believe there are also a few more camping opportunities just past this on the other side of the stream, but I didn't go up to investigate. When you reach the Paria River Confluence, you can either turn left and head out to **White House Campground** via **White House Trail** or you can continue following the Paria River through Paria Canyon toward Lees Ferry. Once you enter Paria Canyon, the canyon walls slowly begin to spread farther apart. You'll follow the river at first (the river may be dry for the first several miles), but soon you'll have the option of cutting up onto sediment deposits around bends as well. You'll still be crossing the river constantly, so don't have any expectation of making it out with dry feet, but you will leave behind the chest-deep slot canyon pools of muck. If you look in the areas on the inside of the river bends, you'll usually be able to find campsites. If you're planning to filter from the springs, pay attention to where they're marked on the map (the map below shows approximate locations only). The springs are not obvious, marked, or necessarily easy to find; I could only find one.
[w3] Paria Canyon Backpacking Guide – Bearfoot Theory
  Tips for pacing a 4-day Paria Canyon hike, including a 3-day alternative, and an overview of the Paria Narrows and Buckskin Gulch side trip.
  We met one couple doing it in 3 days/2 nights. If that is all the time you have, then it is doable, but be prepared for very long days. It’s important to keep in mind that hiking in the river is surprisingly slow, especially if water levels are high. My most recent trip was in late September when the days were shorter. [w3] Paria Canyon Backpacking Guide – Bearfoot Theory
# Paria Canyon Backpacking Guide This is hands down my favorite backpacking trip in Southern Utah. Get the full details on hiking through Paria Canyon here. Located on the Utah/Arizona border in the Paria Canyon-Vermillion Cliffs Wilderness, backpacking Paria Canyon involves 38 miles of hiking down the meandering riverbed in between two enormous walls of Navajo sandstone. I’ve done this backpacking trip twice now – spending four days hiking through this winding, peaceful canyon, and in my opinion, Paria Canyon has the best of what Utah has to offer. A Paria Canyon backpacking trip requires wading downriver, with dozens of crossings – in some ways similar to hiking the Narrows in Zion, but more remote and isolated.

Your feet will be wet the entire time. Due to the nature of the trail (or lack of trail), the hiking is slow, but it is nothing short of spectacular and worth every ounce of effort. What made it even better is that this trail is very quiet. The first time I hiked it, we only saw one other pair of hikers. The second time, we only saw a few small groups on the first and last day. Both times, we had the canyon all to ourselves, meaning that the BLM’s permit process is working well to keep this place wild. In this Paria Canyon Backpacking Guide, I share everything you need to know to plan your own backpacking trip.


## Paria Canyon Hike Overview

#### Trail Basics

###

My Route While there are three different starting trailheads for Paria Canyon, the best way to experience it is a one-way hike from the White House Trailhead near the Paria Contact Station and finish at Lee’s Ferry. This is the route I followed on both of my trips. This route is 38 miles long and gradually loses 1,600 feet in elevation over the course of the trip. The trail is mostly easy to follow, as a majority of the hiking is done in the riverbed. Both times, I did the Paria Canyon hike in 4 days/3 nights and found the pace to be just right. It honestly would have been difficult to do it in less.

We met one couple doing it in 3 days/2 nights. If that is all the time you have, then it is doable, but be prepared for very long days. It’s important to keep in mind that hiking in the river is surprisingly slow, especially if water levels are high. My most recent trip was in late September when the days were shorter. We woke up at 6:30am each day and hiked at a leisurely pace until about 4:30pm. That gave us 2 hours until sunset to set up and enjoy camp.

### Alternative Routes

There are a few alternative routes you might consider, depending on how much time you have and what kind of challenge you are looking for:

If you want to start at White House like I did, you can travel through the Paria Narrows and then still explore a bit of the bottom of Buckskin Gulch once you reach the Confluence on Day 1. While not as constricted as Buckskin Gulch, the walls of the Paria Narrows close in to about 6 feet across at some points, meaning you still get to experience some deep slot canyon hiking. ### Save this post!


## Paria Canyon Map and Navigation

This is the map the ranger will provide you when you pick up your permit at the Paria Contact Station.

You can click on it to view a magnified version. As you can see, it’s not very detailed, and they had no other maps available for sale. While navigation through Paria Canyon is easy (it’s impossible to get lost), there are very few reference points that can help you determine your location. For this reason, I highly recommend you carry a GPS on your trip. To help you, I created a GPS file with the location of the campsites and springs, so you can track your location in real-time on the hike. Download my GPS file here. Just click “Export” and choose GPX, and then you can upload that file to your GPS. If you don’t have a GPS already, I use the Garmin Inreach which is also acts as an emergency satellite communicator.

## Best Time to Hike Paria Canyon Although the canyon is open year-round for backpacking, the air temperatures in late spring and early fall are going to be the most comfortable. These are also the most popular times, so you need to plan far in advance to make sure you get a permit through the lottery system. The risk of flash floods is the highest in July, August, and early September. Flash floods in Paria Canyon, particularly in the Narrows, can be very dangerous since there are places where there is no high ground. In the days leading up to your trip, be sure to check Paria Canyon weather, as well as the weather at Bryce Canyon since rain in Bryce Canyon flows down into the Paria watershed. If the forecast is calling for a chance of rain, call the Rangers station to seek their advice about whether or not it is safe to hike. Even after dry periods, the river banks can be very muddy and slippery. For this reason, I probably wouldn’t do this hike right after a lot of heavy rain. Recent storms mean that the river will be deep, extra muddy, and too silty to filter from.

## Paria Canyon Permits

Permits are required for both day hiking and overnight trips in Paria Canyon and Buckskin Gulch. Walk-up permits are available for day hiking at the trailheads (no limit on day hikers – $6 fee), but overnight permits must be obtained through the Paria Canyon online permit application system. No same-day overnight permits are granted. Permits must be picked up within 10 days of your start date from the Vermillion Cliffs National Monument office in Saint George, the Paria Contact Station, which is right near the White House Trailhead, or the Kanab BLM field office.

The BLM only allows a total of 20 people per day to enter the canyon on overnight permits, and that is across all of the trailheads. There is a $6 reservation fee per group, and an additional $5 permit fee per person per day. Dogs are also allowed for an extra fee of $5 per dog per day. When making a reservation, you will reserve the number of days you plan to spend in the canyon, not nights. For overnight permits, the reservation system opens up at 12pm Mountain Time on the 1st of every month, 3 months before the month of your hike. For example, on February 1 permits for May would open. On the permit application website, the calendar shows you when there is availability. If a date is blue, it means there are permits available to enter the canyon to backpack on that day, and the number shown indicates the number of spaces (one space = one person) that are available. Gray dates mean there are no permits available to start on that day. For the best chance of getting a permit for the busiest spring and fall months, you should plan on being on the website right at noon on the day that permits become available.

## Paria Canyon Trail Campsites

Campsites are spread throughout Paria Canyon and tend to be on sandy beaches above the river. The BLM asks that you choose existing campsites that are at least 200ft away from water and also appear to be worn to avoid creating new sites. It was pretty obvious where most of these campsites were, and you can see the three campsites I stayed at on my first trip marked on the map above. The main thing to take into consideration when camping is the location of the fresh water springs. Depending on how much sediment is in the river, the springs may be the easiest places to obtain water. You will need to filter your water even from the springs, so be sure to bring a backpacking water filter. Campfires are not allowed at any of the sites. Based on my two trips, my recommendations for campsites are:

## Water Availability in Paria Canyon

Water availability is something to take into account when you are planning your Paria Canyon backpacking itinerary, which might seem strange considering you are hiking down a river.

### Filtering from the river

The Paria River can be very silty, and a lot of water filters simply can’t handle the grit and can get clogged.

However, I lucked out on both of my trips. It hadn’t rained for a while, and the water flowing in the river was relatively clear. This meant we were able to filter right out of the river without any issues. Due to animals that live upstream, I’ve heard that if you are going to drink water out of the river, you should both filter and purify it to get rid of bacteria and viruses. We only filtered water and didn’t use a purifier, and neither of us got sick, but if the water had looked dirtier or there had been a lot of recent rain, I would have thrown some purification tablets in just in case. For filtering: I used the CNOC Outdoors 2 liter water container to fill from the river and then ran the water through my Versa Flow Lightweight water filter into my Platypus Soft Bottles. This system is incredibly light, was very fast, and is easy to backflow if it happens to get clogged (which I did not experience). If there is lots of sediment in the river, there are a couple of tricks you can use to prevent your filter from getting clogged. First, you can use a buff, bandana or shirt to pre-filter the water. Next, you can let the water and silt settle in some sort of container before running the water through your filter. You can also bring something called Alum Powder which can be a life saver in the desert. You just add a small amount of alum to the water, and it causes the silt to quickly sink to the bottom.

Once that happens, you can carefully pour the clear water into whatever you are using to treat/filter it.

### Filling up at the springs

If the river is really silty, your best bet is going to be to fill up at the reliable freshwater springs that provide a source of drinking water. These are seeps where the water flows right out of the cracks in the sides of the canyon walls.

This water should also be filtered for safety, but the sediment won’t be an issue. Many of the springs are easy to miss, so it’s important to be on the close lookout. Lush vegetation growing out of the canyon walls is a sign that a spring might be present. The most reliable springs are marked on the map above (and on the GPS file) and are located at:

Please note water access may have changed since I was there – always check with a ranger before heading out for the most up-to-date water information. If you can’t easily filter from the river, camping at sites near these springs is best because it means you don’t have to carry additional water for cooking your backpacking meals. You just fill up when you arrive at camp and before you leave in the morning. In this case, I’d recommend carrying at least 4-5 liters per person to get you from one spring to the next. It should be noted that you should fill up all of your water bottles at the Last Reliable Spring.

Beyond that, the trail has virtually no shade and can be very hot.

**Short answer: treat it as an out-and-back side trip from the confluence, done without your pack.**

Here's how it works in practice:

- From the [White House Trailhead](N6404659104) you walk down the Paria riverbed; the canyon tightens into the Narrows around mile 4, and you hit the [Buckskin Gulch & Paria River Confluence](N1458539830) at roughly mile 7 — a very reasonable Day 1 if you're camping, and the usual lunch/rest point if you're pushing through.
- At the junction, turn **right (north/upstream)** into Buckskin rather than continuing down the Paria. Drop your pack at the confluence — there are established campsites on the sand and on the elevated ramp just above the junction, which is the first safe camp coming down Buckskin.
- The honest expectation: this is a *taste*, not a tour. [Bearfoot Theory](w3) describes spending about 20 minutes walking up Buckskin before the water got too deep — and Buckskin's pools are deeper and muckier than the Paria's. Budget 30–45 minutes round trip and accept that you'll stop at the first chest-deep pool.
- One obstacle to know about: just above the confluence there's a short 15–20 ft downclimb with a fixed rope and shallow moqui steps cut into the rock, which [Halfway Anywhere](w2) flags as insecure and awkward — especially with a pack or a dog. Going upstream you'll meet it head-on, so if it looks bad, that's your turnaround point. Leaving the pack behind is what makes this safe and quick.
- Two cautions. First, [Bearfoot Theory](w3) notes flash-flood risk peaks July–early September and the Narrows has stretches with no high ground — a side trip into an even tighter slot on a marginal weather day isn't worth it. Second, if you truly want Buckskin, the superior version is to descend the whole gulch from Wire Pass and exit via White House, as [365atlantatraveler](w4) outlines; a confluence side trip is a sampler.

So: reach the confluence on Day 1, stash your pack, walk up Buckskin for 15–30 minutes until the water or the rope climb stops you, then come back and camp at the junction before continuing down the Paria to White House.

**Yes — that's Agios Neophytos Monastery (Saint Neophytos Monastery), and it's the classic quick day trip from Paphos.**

The saint in question is Neophytos, a 12th-century Cypriot recluse. According to [Wikipedia](w6), the monastery stands in the territory of the village of Tala, about 1 km north of the village and roughly 15 km north of Paphos. Neophytos came here in the mid-12th century after fleeing into the hills to pursue an ascetic life; in 1159 he found a small cave and began carving it out himself to make a hermit's cell, a chapel and eventually his own tomb — the cave hermitage ("Enkleistra") with its painted frescoes is still the highlight of a visit, as the [Dominique travels](w1) account of the hermit-founder describes. A small community of monks grew up around his retreat ([Man Vs Globe](w2)).

**How far from Paphos:** the monastery's ref in the places database sits at roughly 8 km as the crow flies from central Paphos (I measured 8.1 km from the town centre), which works out to about 15 km by road on the winding climb up to Tala. Travel writers put it at roughly a 20–30 minute drive from Paphos, which the [nomadasaurus](w3) guide confirms as "only a 30 minutes drive" — so it's an easy half-day or less.

Practical notes: no photography or videography is allowed on site ([theworldpursuit](w4)), and it's a serene alternative if you'd rather skip a boat day ([atlifestylecrossroads](w5)). If you want a longer mountain drive, Kykkos Monastery is another famous house (about 33 km from Paphos, open daily 10:00–17:00), but it was founded under Byzantine imperial patronage rather than by a hermit — so Agios Neophytos is the one that matches your question.

**Yes — that's Agios Neophytos Monastery (Saint Neophytos Monastery), and it's the classic quick day trip from Paphos.**

The saint in question is Neophytos, a 12th-century Cypriot recluse. According to [Wikipedia](w6), the monastery stands in the territory of the village of Tala, about 1 km north of the village and roughly 15 km north of Paphos. Neophytos came here in the mid-12th century after fleeing into the hills to pursue an ascetic life; in 1159 he found a small cave and began carving it out himself to make a hermit's cell, a chapel and eventually his own tomb — the cave hermitage ("Enkleistra") with its painted frescoes is still the highlight of a visit, as the [Dominique travels](w1) account of the hermit-founder describes. A small community of monks grew up around his retreat ([Man Vs Globe](w2)).

**How far from Paphos:** the monastery's ref in the places database sits at roughly 8 km as the crow flies from central Paphos (I measured 8.1 km from the town centre), which works out to about 15 km by road on the winding climb up to Tala. Travel writers put it at roughly a 20–30 minute drive from Paphos, which the [nomadasaurus](w3) guide confirms as "only a 30 minutes drive" — so it's an easy half-day or less.

Practical notes: no photography or videography is allowed on site ([theworldpursuit](w4)), and it's a serene alternative if you'd rather skip a boat day ([atlifestylecrossroads](w5)). If you want a longer mountain drive, Kykkos Monastery is another famous house (about 33 km from Paphos, open daily 10:00–17:00), but it was founded under Byzantine imperial patronage rather than by a hermit — so Agios Neophytos is the one that matches your question.

## Getting from Ramstein to Nanstein Castle

**The short version:** it's a very easy half-day trip — the castle sits on the ridge right above Landstuhl, only about 6 km from Ramstein.

**By train + walk (no car needed)**
- Take the S-Bahn/regional train from **Ramstein station** (Bahnhofstraße, in the town centre) one stop to **Landstuhl station** — a ride of just a few minutes on the Kaiserslautern–Homburg line.
- From Landstuhl station it's roughly a 1.5 km uphill walk (20–30 minutes) through town and then forest paths to the castle gate. The climb is steady but short.

**By car**
- About 10 minutes via the B37/L395 through Landstuhl. There's a free car park right at the castle, which connects directly to the marked forest loops — the main loop is about 2.5 km and mostly flat, per [kimberlykepharttravels.com](w8), who rates Nanstein as the closest easy outing to Ramstein for families.

**At the castle**
Burg Nanstein is a 12th-century red-sandstone ruin above Landstuhl, partially reconstructed, with towers to climb, cellars and dungeons to poke around, and a 360° view over the Palatinate Forest from the top. Right at the entrance is **Burgschänke Nanstein**, a cosy restaurant serving warm meals all day — [RaulersonGirlsTravel](w7) had sausage and sauerkraut there for €7.90.

**Practical notes — and one discrepancy worth knowing**
- [RaulersonGirlsTravel](w7) reports opening hours of Tue–Sun 10–4 (Oct–Mar) and 9–6 (Apr–Sep), **closed Mondays**, with a small admission fee (about €3 adult / €2.10 child, with discounts for military, students, seniors and disabled visitors).
- [kimberlykepharttravels.com](w8) instead describes the ruins as freely accessible with no ticket required and only 20–30 minutes needed to explore.
- These two accounts conflict, so treat the fee and Monday closure as "check on arrival" — the grounds are walkable either way, and the castle is not wheelchair accessible.

**My suggested plan:** morning train from Ramstein to Landstuhl, walk up, spend an hour or two exploring the ruins and the viewpoint, lunch at the Burgschänke, then walk back down for the return train. Total time out: about half a day.

## Getting from Ramstein to Nanstein Castle

**The short version:** it's a very easy half-day trip — the castle sits on the ridge right above Landstuhl, only about 6 km from Ramstein.

**By train + walk (no car needed)**
- Take the S-Bahn/regional train from **Ramstein station** (Bahnhofstraße, in the town centre) one stop to **Landstuhl station** — a ride of just a few minutes on the Kaiserslautern–Homburg line.
- From Landstuhl station it's roughly a 1.5 km uphill walk (20–30 minutes) through town and then forest paths to the castle gate. The climb is steady but short.

**By car**
- About 10 minutes via the B37/L395 through Landstuhl. There's a free car park right at the castle, which connects directly to the marked forest loops — the main loop is about 2.5 km and mostly flat, per [kimberlykepharttravels.com](w8), who rates Nanstein as the closest easy outing to Ramstein for families.

**At the castle**
Burg Nanstein is a 12th-century red-sandstone ruin above Landstuhl, partially reconstructed, with towers to climb, cellars and dungeons to poke around, and a 360° view over the Palatinate Forest from the top. Right at the entrance is **Burgschänke Nanstein**, a cosy restaurant serving warm meals all day — [RaulersonGirlsTravel](w7) had sausage and sauerkraut there for €7.90.

**Practical notes — and one discrepancy worth knowing**
- [RaulersonGirlsTravel](w7) reports opening hours of Tue–Sun 10–4 (Oct–Mar) and 9–6 (Apr–Sep), **closed Mondays**, with a small admission fee (about €3 adult / €2.10 child, with discounts for military, students, seniors and disabled visitors).
- [kimberlykepharttravels.com](w8) instead describes the ruins as freely accessible with no ticket required and only 20–30 minutes needed to explore.
- These two accounts conflict, so treat the fee and Monday closure as "check on arrival" — the grounds are walkable either way, and the castle is not wheelchair accessible.

**My suggested plan:** morning train from Ramstein to Landstuhl, walk up, spend an hour or two exploring the ruins and the viewpoint, lunch at the Burgschänke, then walk back down for the return train. Total time out: about half a day.

**The short answer: there is no train to Dharamkot itself — the railhead is Pathankot, and the rest is road.**

**The route**
1. **Overnight express, Old Delhi → Pathankot Junction** (~10–12 h). Travel writers consistently name this as the standard move: one [Drifter Planet](w3) guide says she has "taken an overnight train from Delhi to Pathankot station" repeatedly and prefers the **Dhauladhar Express** for its timings, while a [Trekking to Triund](w1) guide simply says "take an overnight train from Delhi to Pathankot." Other Delhi–Pathankot expresses (including the Delhi–Pathankot Superfast Express, [Wikipedia](w9)) cover the same run — aim to arrive Pathankot early morning.
2. **Pathankot → McLeod Ganj**, either a taxi (about 2.5 h) or a local bus (4–5 h, stopping in every village). Both figures come from [Drifter Planet](w3), and a [Where and Wander](w5) account describes doing it by car in roughly three bumpy hours after a sleepless overnight train.
3. **McLeod Ganj → Dharamkot**, the last leg. The bus drops you at McLeod Ganj bus stand, not up in the village; from there it's a 15–20 minute walk on the shortcut (longer with luggage) or a short auto-rickshaw hop, per [Drifter Planet](w3) and [Global Gallivanting](w2). Alternatively skip the bus leg entirely and take a taxi straight through to Dharamkot.

**The scenic alternative (no good for reaching Dharamkot directly)**
Some trains stop at **Chakki Bank** instead of Pathankot Junction — the two are only about 5 km apart, per [Solo Backpacker](w4). From the narrow-gauge **Pathankot Junction (NG)** platform you can ride the **Kangra Valley Railway** toy train up to **Kangra Mandir** (with views over Pong Dam), but that line heads toward Joginder Nagar, away from Dharamshala — you'd then need a bus or auto down to Kangra bus stand and on to McLeod Ganj. Treat it as a side trip for the scenery, not the fast route, as [Drifter Planet](w1) also frames it.

**Practical notes**
- Booking a bus direct from Delhi to McLeod Ganj (~₹1000–1300, departing late afternoon/evening from ISBT Kashmere Gate) is the no-hassle rival to the train, per [Drifter Planet](w1) and [Drifter Planet](w3).
- Nearest airport if you'd rather fly is Kangra Gaggal (DHM), served from Delhi.
- Once at Pathankot, don't count on booking onward transport late; morning arrival makes the bus/taxi leg much smoother.

Dharamshala is a famous Buddhist destinations in Himachal Pradesh, India. Both Dharamshala and McLeodganj have become extremely crowded because they are popular summer travel destinations. However, the nearby Dharamkot has managed to maintain its quaint charm. It is the place where you can get spiritual, Dharamkot is the perfect little Yoga village and is ideal for a few days’ time off from the real world.

Or even months.. if you’re lucky enough to take time off work for that long. Dharamkot is the perfect base for multiple hikes in the Himalayas such as Triund, Illaqua, Indrahar Pass, etc. It is just an overnight bus ride away from the famous backpackers’ hot spot – Kasol. My first visit to this village was back in 2008 and I went back total 5 times for more. ## Is Dharamkot for you (Maybe Not)

If you’re looking for a relaxed vacation that doesn’t involve hiking or walking around, then Dharamkot is NOT the place for you. **This village doesn’t have any roads, except for a single road that leads to it** and pretty much ends at “Trek and Dine” –  a famous café. After Trek N Dine, the road narrows down to a pathway, ideal for aimless walks through the village to various other view points, rocks, waterfalls and some treks.

[toc]

## Where is Dharamkot? Dharamkot is in Kangra Valley in Himachal Pradesh state of India. As mentioned before, it is near the more famous Dharamshala and McLeodganj.

## How to reach Dharamkot:

### Reaching Dharamkot by Air

The nearest airport to Dharamkot is Kangra Gaggal Airport, which is also called Dharamshala airport. The airport code is DHM. AllianceAir and Spicejet run flights from here to and from Delhi, Jaipur and Kanpur. The Kanga Gaggal airport is newly constructed and we loved it. We saw an amazing view of the snow covered Dhauladhar Mountains as we boarded our SpiceJet flight to Delhi from here.

### Reaching Dharamkot by Train from Delhi

On most occasions, I have taken an overnight train from Delhi to Pathankot station in order to reach Dharamkot. There are many trains but I prefer Dhalaudhar Express because of the timings.

I love to sleep! There are two options to reach Dharamkot from Pathankot – take a taxi to Dharamkot or a local bus to McLeodganj. The taxi takes around 2.5 hours depending on the traffic and the buses take 4 to 5 hours since they stop at many villages to pick up people and make more money. I have traveled by both. If you decide to travel by a local bus, it will most likely drop you in McLeodganj, not Dharamkot. You can walk to Dharamkot in 20 minutes from McLeodganj or just take an auto-rickshaw or a taxi. to I have been to McLeodganj a few times while I was a student, so I usually skip this place all together because it has become extremely crowded and is no longer a backpacker destination. ### Reaching Dharamkot by Bus from Delhi

It is very easy to reach Dharamkot by bus. You can also take a direct overnight bus from Delhi to McLeodganj. A decent bus will cost you around INR 1000 – 1200 per person but I prefer the trains.

### McLeodganj to Dharamkot

From McLeodganj bus stop, there’s a short cut to Dharamkot which will take you 15 minutes to cover if you walk at a leisurely pace, and 20 if you’re carrying luggage and are tired from a bumpy butt breaking bus journey from Pathankot. Ask anyone at the bus station to point you to the right direction since most of the people here understand English. Upon reaching Dharamkot, you can replenish your energy at any one of the beautiful cafes. I have never had a bad meal or a bad cup of coffee or tea in this area.

## Where to Stay in Dharamkot

A few years back, I would have told you to reach Dharamkot without a room and find one here.

However things have changed a little since then. I highly recommend a place called Dharamkot Inn, which is just at the beginning on Dharamkot. We picked this place because we didn’t want to hike with our luggage and our 5 month old baby. This is one of the rare places in Dharamkot where you can reach on a taxi till the door. Moreover, you can also get hot water in Dharamkot Inn because they have solar powered heating system. You can also also check out the deals on Mountain view budget Stay on Booking.com. Based on the feedback from our friends, here are more places that we recommend you check out – Shiv Shakti guest house (Dharamkot), the Lodge (Dharamkot), Kamal guest house (Dharamkot road, McLeod ganj), Gandhi’s paradise (Dharamkot road,McLeod ganj), and the Castle (Bhagsu village). If you arrive here without a booking, the just keep in mind that the room rates are obviously high at the entry point, i.e., **Trek and Dine** (Upper Dharamkot) and they get cheaper as the road becomes smaller (Lower Dharamkot). If you’re lucky, you can even find a twin room with a toilet for as low as INR 500 per night inside the village.

## The Vibe in Dharamkot:

The best thing about Dharamkot is the vibe. Let me try to describe the vibe here if I can. The vibe is a mix of some of magic, pure spiritual energy of the Himalayas, happiness of the simple folks that live there, peace & serenity and a feeling on oneness with the nature. The sounds of mountain birds, the whistling of air through deodar tree leaves, the distant smells of farm animals mixed with herb-based cooking will awaken all your senses. This is a good spot for early morning yoga and meditation – if you’re in that sort of stuff.

## The Food in Dharamkot – What to Eat (and Where)

### Everything in Trek N Dine (esp Shakshuka, Wood Fired Pizza and Lasagna) Most of the destinations on the banana pancake trail usually have cafes with really good food but I think Dharamkot takes the highest spot on my list. A lot of Israeli, European and Tibetans frequently visit Dharamkot and many have decided to live here. As a result, every single café that I have ever visited here have totally nailed their lasagnas, pastas, pancakes, hummus and Shakshuka. Strangely, the Indian food in Dharamkot is not very appealing. Of course Dharamkot has many places to eat but there is a reason why Trek N Dine is the most popular place. You will simply never have a bad meal here. I often try to avoid famous places and spend more time in smaller ones but I make an exception with Trek N Dine.

### Fresh Mint, Ginger and Lemon tea with Honey

The herbal teas – usually ginger, lemon, honey and mint was our regular beverage everywhere.

You will get this in almost every single cafe and they will pluck out fresh mint leaves and put them in the hot water long with freshly grated ginger and a slice of lemon.

### Yak Cheese Sandwich in Lama Cafe

Ever seen Yaks? These hairy sisters of buffaloes are super adorable and live in the Himalayas. Called Chhurpi in Nepalese, the Yak cheese tastes like Gouda and you can taste it in Lama Cafe in Dharamkot. This little Nepalese cafe has some really amazing cakes, cookies, coffee and of course Yak cheese sandwiches.

### Bhagsu Cake

The most amazing dessert to eat in this area is a dessert called **Bhagsu cake**. Bhagsu cake has a typical crunchy pie crust, layered with sticky caramel toffee sauce and topped with dark chocolate or white chocolate.

Seriously, we couldn’t get enough of this and tried this at almost every café. The dark chocolate one is almost everywhere, but the white one was only available at one place – it’s a shop between Milky Way Galaxy café and Trek and Dine Café. Our favorite place for Bhagsu Cake was **Moonlight Cafe**. Just so you know, Bhagsu is the name of a nearby village, which is famous for a waterfall and a temple – both extremely crowded.

### Vegan Food in Blue Caterpillar and Once in Nature

To continue my talk about the awesome food in this area, I must mention how presently surprised we were to discover a few **Vegan cafes** in this village. The most famous one is towards the other side of the village, on the way to Bhagsu near the rocks. It’s very easy to find this because you will find many rocks with “Vegan Café” painted on them and they will lead you to this place. When we visited, there was live trance music and a few traveling artists with their work on display. There were a few other vegan cafes around as well. Do check out **Blue Caterpillar** and **Once in Nature** if you’re a Vegan. Personally, I tried to be a Vegan for a few weeks but had to give up because I can’t quit Honey.

### Momos

I love momos. Momos are Tibetan dumplings that are usually stuffed with pork, chicken or veggies. What better place to eat Tibetan food than Dharamkot. You can find them in many places all over Dharamkot, but again I had the best ones in Trek N Dine. ### The Best Coffee (Espresso and Cappuccino) in Dharamkot?

Trek N Dine My husband is half Italian and half German so the Italian in him is always very critical of coffee and to his surprise, Trek and Dine’s **espresso** was perfect.

## Drinking in Dharamkot:

If you like drinking light alcohol, you can try some of the few Himalayan fruit wines and apple cedar which you will easily find in the grocery shops for INR 200 – 300. My favorite was the peach wine but the shopkeeper insisted I try Kiwi as well which was the highest selling. Everything herbal is available in plenty so if you want, you can skip alcohol altogether.

## Things to do in Dharamkot:

### 01) Get Lost in the village

My recommendation to everyone who’s visiting this little paradise is to walk around and get lost in the area. Who knows what you may come across? If you discover new a viewpoint, waterfall, or just anything else, let me know! We got lost and found a meditation spot on top of a hill in the middle of nowhere with Buddhist flags and a hand painted message on a rock.

### 02) Visit Gallu and Admire the Breathtaking Views

You can hike to the nearby village Gallu and admire the breathtaking views from a cafe on top of the hill here. Ask anyone the way to Gallu temple and they will point you in the right direction. The hike from Dharamkot to Gallu is easy and will not take more than 20 minutes. Read my guide to Gallu for more information.

### 03) Trek to the “no name waterfall” (near Gallu)

Up for some more adventure? From Gallu, you can also hike for one hour and reach an **amazing waterfall** which is usually empty, unlike Bhagsu’s super crowded waterfall. The hike to this waterfall is super slippery, so please wear good hiking shoes and be comfortable. Carry a swimsuit if you want to take a dip here.

### 04)

Walk to Bhagsu Village from Dharamkot

There are two ways of reaching Bhagsu village from Dharamkot. First, you can hire a took took (auto rickshaw) from Dharamkot’s main road for Bhagsu. Second, there is a shortcut that leads to Bhagsu village from Dharamkot. The hike from Dharamkot to Bhagsu beautiful and simple. You just need to walk towards the vegan cafe and after you cross it, you will be inside Bhagsu village. Bhagu is famous for a massive waterfall, hippie cafes and a temple. It is definitely not my favorite area because its usually crowded.

### 05)

Trek to Triund and camp there overnight

Triund is four hours hike away from Dharamkot. I recommend you start this hike very early in the morning and camp at Triund at night. You don’t have to carry a tent because it is possible to rent one there. The hike is almost fully uphill and is strenuous.

For more information, read my travel guide for Triund.

### 06) Visit the Monasteries and Temples in McLeodganj and Dharamshala In order to reach Dharamkot, you will first reach McLeodganj and Dharamshala. Yes, these two towns are crowded and don’t have Dharamkot’s relaxed vibe. However, if you want to visit the famous Buddhist temples and Monasteries here, you can make a day trip. Did you know that the Dalai Lama lives in Dharamshala? If you’re lucky, maybe you can meet him! Oh also, Dharamshala has India’s highest cricket
